audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated non-site-admin with the perm_template permission can GET the event-template add page (or edit a template writable by that user's organisation). EventTemplatesController::__setBuilderConfig() queried every enabled Galaxy row without Galaxy visibility conditions, grouped the results by type, retained each type and description, and embedded that data in window.ET_BUILDER_CONFIG.multipickerSources. Consequently, the builder response disclosed metadata for enabled private distribution-0 galaxies owned by other organisations.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea introduced the galaxy-type picker and, in the same atomic feature commit, first added the server-side Galaxy->find('all') with only 'Galaxy.enabled' => true. It did not call Galaxy::buildConditions() or otherwise restrict by the requesting user's organisation/distribution before exposing Galaxy.type and Galaxy.description to the browser.
audit_record.ai_marker: BIC commit object contains the exact trailer 'Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>'. git cat-file -p also shows human author and committer iglocska <andras.iklody@gmail.com>; the Claude Co-Authored-By trailer is nevertheless explicit commit-object AI co-authorship.
evidence: First-party advisory https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3636-3mqq-q7x9 describes non-site-admin access to private galaxies from other organisations through event-template creation, names leaked galaxy type/description metadata, and references d3adfe1a097dd4b403364e9af34e208660eeec1a; its affected/patched version fields are Unknown.

git show 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea -- app/Controller/EventTemplatesController.php shows the BIC adding __setBuilderConfig()'s Galaxy->find('all') with conditions array('Galaxy.enabled' => true), fields Galaxy.type and Galaxy.description, grouping by Galaxy.type, and set('galaxyTypesAvailable', ...). The same commit wires those values into the event-template builder's browser configuration.

git log -S"'Galaxy.enabled' => true" -- app/Controller/EventTemplatesController.php resolves the first addition to 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea. git log -L over the added galaxy-result processing also traces those lines to that commit. git cat-file -p shows it is a normal one-parent commit, parent 66f278bb2be0e8183d56eede615d7cc370f38303, so no squash/member decomposition is needed.

Immediate-parent tree verification: git grep -n -E 'galaxyTypesAvailable|Galaxy\.enabled|loadModel\(.Galaxy.' 66f278bb2be0e8183d56eede615d7cc370f38303 -- app/Controller/EventTemplatesController.php returned no matches (exit 1), while the parent-to-BIC diff adds the entire unrestricted Galaxy query and result exposure. The vulnerable mechanism is therefore absent from the direct parent.

Authorization/reachability: app/Controller/Component/ACLComponent.php grants eventTemplates/add and eventTemplates/edit to perm_template users; EventTemplatesController.php calls __setBuilderConfig() on GET add and GET edit. Thus a low-privileged authenticated template author can receive the leaked picker configuration; edit additionally enforces own-organisation ownership of the template, which does not constrain the separate Galaxy query.

The advisory-referenced d3adfe1a097dd4b403364e9af34e208660eeec1a is an incomplete attempted repair: it adds an OR condition containing 'Galaxy.distribution' > 0, which PHP evaluates before building the query rather than expressing a CakePHP field comparison. The later effective fix 8aa2bb6d1af6e8c57c8d8437cf203acb8bce7a53 explicitly identifies that expression as an always-true PHP comparison and replaces the hand-written condition with $this->Galaxy->buildConditions($this->Auth->user()). Galaxy.php's buildConditions() permits site admins globally and otherwise limits results to default galaxies, the user's org, or non-private distributions 1-3.

Version boundary from repository tags: git tag --contains 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea starts at v2.5.37, and git grep finds no Galaxy.enabled query in v2.5.36 but finds it in v2.5.37/v2.5.38. d3adfe1a097dd4b403364e9af34e208660eeec1a first appears in v2.5.39, which still contains the malformed comparison. 8aa2bb6d1af6e8c57c8d8437cf203acb8bce7a53 first appears in v2.5.40; git grep finds the canonical buildConditions call in v2.5.40 and not v2.5.39. Therefore the shipped vulnerable boundary is v2.5.37 through v2.5.39, with the effective patched boundary at v2.5.40.

git merge-base --is-ancestor confirms both the BIC and the advisory-referenced attempted fix are ancestors of 8aa2bb6d1af6e8c57c8d8437cf203acb8bce7a53. git show/cat-file of the BIC itself provides the only AI attribution used here: the exact Claude Opus Co-Authored-By trailer on the commit that first wrote the flawed query.
audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerability begins when 47bf71cc78d13c06e1eaa4d9842e6f94ddce4bea turns the galaxy restriction input into a populated picker. Its server-side data source selects all enabled galaxies and exports type/description values without applying the Galaxy model's existing visibility policy. The GET add/edit routes make that data reachable to authenticated non-admin template authors. History searches identify this commit, rather than the earlier controller scaffold or later moves/refactors, as the smallest BIC; direct inspection of 66f278bb2be0e8183d56eede615d7cc370f38303 proves the query and exposure are absent there. Tag membership puts introduction after v2.5.36 and in v2.5.37. The referenced d3adfe1a097dd4b403364e9af34e208660eeec1a attempts an organisation/distribution filter but writes the distribution predicate as a PHP boolean expression, leaving the disclosure open in v2.5.39. Commit 8aa2bb6d1af6e8c57c8d8437cf203acb8bce7a53 directly closes the mechanism by using Galaxy::buildConditions(), and v2.5.40 is the first tag containing that effective repair. Because the BIC commit object explicitly credits Claude Opus as co-author and that same commit first wrote the causally flawed unrestricted query, the BIC-only rule yields AI_ROOT_CAUSE.

audit_record.bug_semantics: A scoped access token carrying only profile:read is accepted by PUT /user because that mutating route is guarded by RequireScopes(ScopeProfileRead). UpdateUser uses the token viewer's administrator identity and permits a supplied password to replace that administrator's password. The attacker can then log in with the replacement password; login issues a session JWT, and RequireScopes deliberately bypasses scope checks for session tokens, yielding unrestricted administrator access.
audit_record.flaw_origin: PR #195 introduced route-level scoped-token authorization. Its member b47fa1c75d890cd080e3f6699bbfca8cd8d4b939 first wrote the causal mismatch in internal/router/user.go by binding PUT /user to ScopeProfileRead. GitHub later landed the PR as squash commit 3f8fb150158723aca31df2ae937a1aa7b31ac254; that mainline aggregate carries the flaw but is not the smallest BIC.
audit_record.ai_marker: The exact BIC commit object has human author and committer L1nSn0w <l1nsn0w@qq.com> and the explicit message trailer "Made-with: Cursor". It has no AI author, AI co-author, Co-Authored-By trailer, or Generated-with trailer. This is BIC-local evidence of AI assistance, but not evidence that the AI was the sole author or independently identifiable root cause.
evidence: The first-party advisory https://github.com/lin-snow/Ech0/security/advisories/GHSA-hm2h-wwwh-g49x states the precise escalation chain: profile:read token -> PUT /user password change -> login -> unrestricted session token. It identifies the flawed RequireScopes("profile:read") guard, the password assignment, the session-token scope bypass, and patched version 4.4.3.

The GitHub commit API object for b47fa1c75d890cd080e3f6699bbfca8cd8d4b939 reports sole parent 1b280c252d1ef2ee69bf09f890d2da673b4b0a68 and its internal/router/user.go patch directly changes the pre-existing one-line PUT /user route to call middleware.RequireScopes(authModel.ScopeProfileRead) before UpdateUser. This is the smallest causal member, not an import, move, refactor, release commit, or squash aggregate.

Direct parent-tree check of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/lin-snow/Ech0/1b280c252d1ef2ee69bf09f890d2da673b4b0a68/internal/router/user.go shows PUT /user calling UpdateUser with no authModel import, RequireScopes call, or ScopeProfileRead mapping. The exact vulnerable authorization contract is absent from the immediate parent.

In the validated clone, git show 3f8fb150158723aca31df2ae937a1aa7b31ac254 -- internal/router/user.go shows the same flawed PUT /user -> ScopeProfileRead mapping arriving in the one-parent mainline squash. audit_record.bug_semantics: OracleIntegration's post-CREATE/post-UPDATE path performs a second SELECT by the driver-produced response.lastRowid. It directly interpolated the Oracle table name, obtained verbatim from user_tables.TABLE_NAME, between double quotes without doubling an embedded double quote. A crafted quoted table name can therefore terminate the identifier and inject SQL executed with the configured datasource user's privileges; response.lastRowid is not the injection vector.

review_record.bug_semantics: Second-order Oracle SQL identifier injection in the post-CREATE/post-UPDATE row lookup. Oracle table names are read verbatim from user_tables.TABLE_NAME and carried into the external-table query metadata. When Oracle returns response.lastRowid, OracleIntegration.query constructs SELECT * FROM "<table name>" WHERE ROWID = '<driver-produced ROWID>' by direct interpolation. An embedded double quote in the table name terminates the quoted identifier and makes the remainder SQL syntax. A user able to write that external table can trigger the lookup; the injected SQL runs with the configured Oracle datasource user's privileges and can cross Budibase's table/row authorization boundary. response.lastRowid is not the attacker-controlled part.
review_record.flaw_origin: 115fc08aa4d08ca08c65c84e3805c6df0e1ea0b8 is the smallest real origin: it replaced the prior returning implementation with a post-write ROWID lookup and first wrote the raw quoted-identifier interpolation, initially using json.endpoint.entityId. At that revision ExternalRequest derives endpoint.entityId directly from tableName, while Oracle schema introspection stores row.TABLE_NAME verbatim, so the original line already has the same identifier-injection semantics. dbe9eedcbadc6d164447078039801a53a2dcfa65 later changed the expression from json.endpoint.entityId to json.table.name but preserved the unsafe double-quote interpolation; it is a source-name rewrite, not the BIC.

audit_record.bug_semantics: PUT /api/global/users/tenant/owner performed a top-privilege identity mutation without an internal-or-admin authorization check. Its cloudRestricted middleware validated an internal API key only when neither SELF_HOSTED nor DISABLE_ACCOUNT_PORTAL was set; in those self-hosted/account-portal-disabled modes it simply called next(). The router-wide guard then admitted any authenticated user with budibaseAccess, including BASIC users. The handler accepted attacker-controlled originalEmail, newAccountEmail, and tenantIds, changed the account-holder's email, and saved with isAccountHolder:true and allowChangingEmail:true, enabling email reassignment followed by the public password-reset flow and administrator takeover where SMTP is configured.

primary_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated application user with TABLE/READ permission and a datasource ID can call GET /api/datasources/:datasourceId. The controller returns the datasource configuration after a schema-type-driven redaction pass, but MongoDB connectionString and Firebase privateKey were declared STRING while holding live credentials. Because removeSecrets masked only PASSWORD and SENSITIVE_LONGFORM fields, those STRING values survived and were returned in plaintext.

Its parent had the controller and TABLE/READ route skeleton, but the parameter mismatch prevented that lookup. At the BIC, MongoDB already stored connectionString as FIELD_TYPES.STRING; Firebase later extended the same flaw in c2d48bebd7100d7949de4555759de543a00b9256 by defining privateKey as STRING. The 2023 redaction addition b659060beb4246ad943b4660fb06f7a823d12a3d was only a partial mitigation and did not originate the reachable TABLE/READ exposure.

review_record.bug_semantics: Budibase's datasource read APIs returned the stored datasource config to an authenticated caller. The later removeSecrets control only replaced fields declared PASSWORD (and, from May 2026, SENSITIVE_LONGFORM), while MongoDB connectionString and Firestore privateKey remained declared STRING. Consequently GET /api/datasources/:datasourceId, authorized only for TABLE/READ in affected code, returned a live MongoDB URI or Firebase service-account private key in plaintext; the builder-only list/read responses were affected by the same schema/redactor mismatch.
review_record.flaw_origin: The complete exploitable path first appears in merge-resolution commit 29b51bc6c2fc8874ab7aa7a0c849ff5f205aec5a: it creates the datasource controller and a TABLE/READ GET /api/datasources/:id route, and find performs database.get(id) followed by ctx.body = datasource with no secret removal. MongoDB's STRING connectionString already existed from fbf501aebc0a4b16e5715e0b4fc875a4998f319b, so 29b51bc6c2fc8874ab7aa7a0c849ff5f205aec5a is the smallest first commit that completed the low-privilege disclosure path. Firebase commit c2d48bebd7100d7949de4555759de543a00b9256 later added privateKey as STRING. Partial-redaction commit b659060beb4246ad943b4660fb06f7a823d12a3d routed reads through removeSecrets but masked only PASSWORD fields, preserving rather than originating the already-exploitable leak.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Ech0 globally installed its i18n middleware and passed unauthenticated request-controlled locale values, including the raw Accept-Language header after only TrimSpace, to go-i18n and golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage without a size or shape bound. The x/text CVE-2022-32149 mitigation counted '-' separators but the parser also aliases '_' to '-', so a near-1 MiB malformed underscore-separated value bypassed the guard and exercised quadratic parsing, allowing unauthenticated CPU denial of service on every route. X-Locale and the lang query parameter also reached the same unbounded parser through ResolveLocale.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit b55edabd228d3de41e781bd3100f2e1ee0835516 first created Ech0's complete remotely reachable vulnerable path: it added internal/i18n/i18n.go, forwarded unbounded locale values to ParseAcceptLanguage and goi18n.NewLocalizer, read Accept-Language from the request, and registered the middleware globally. The parser weakness pre-existed in x/text, but the immediate parent did not contain Ech0's i18n parser path or global exposure.

primary_record.bug_semantics: Ech0 globally ran its i18n middleware before every route and accepted an unauthenticated request's raw Accept-Language value with only TrimSpace. The value reached golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage both directly through ResolveLocale and indirectly through go-i18n's NewLocalizer. x/text's CVE-2022-32149 guard counted '-' but not '_', although its scanner later treats '_' as '-', so a near-1 MiB header composed of malformed underscore-separated tags bypassed the guard and repeatedly exercised the quadratic gobble/memmove path, consuming seconds of CPU per request and enabling denial of service.
primary_record.flaw_origin: Commit b55edabd228d3de41e781bd3100f2e1ee0835516 introduced the entire backend i18n path: internal/i18n/i18n.go added ResolveLocale, the unsanitized goi18n.NewLocalizer wrapper, and Middleware reading Accept-Language, while internal/router/middleware.go installed that middleware globally. Thus the application's exposure originated when attacker-controlled header input was first connected to the vulnerable parser without a size or shape bound; the parser defect itself pre-existed in x/text.

The same commit changes internal/router/middleware.go to call `r.Use(i18nUtil.Middleware())` globally and adds go-i18n/v2 v2.6.1; its resolved x/text dependency is v0.34.0. Direct parent-tree verification with `git ls-tree -r b00c0f7da80cdbf4f4bd84a0c557ae03c88775a6 -- internal/i18n/i18n.go internal/router/middleware.go` returns only internal/router/middleware.go, and `git show b00c0f7da80cdbf4f4bd84a0c557ae03c88775a6:internal/router/middleware.go` has no i18n import or registration. review_record.bug_semantics: Ech0 installed internal/i18n.Middleware() on the global Gin router, so every unauthenticated request supplied its raw, trimmed Accept-Language header to NewLocalizer. NewLocalizer passed that unbounded value directly to go-i18n, whose tag parsing reaches golang.org/x/text/language.ParseAcceptLanguage. The x/text CVE-2022-32149 guard counts '-' separators but the scanner also aliases '_' to '-', so a near-1 MiB header made from malformed underscore-separated subtags bypasses the guard and exercises quadratic gobble/memmove behavior. The same unbounded parser was also reachable through X-Locale and the lang query parameter via ResolveLocale, with those explicit-locale paths potentially adding another parse. This is an unauthenticated CPU denial of service on public routes.
review_record.flaw_origin: Application-boundary flaw first created by b55edabd228d3de41e781bd3100f2e1ee0835516: that single ordinary commit added the i18n implementation, directly forwarded acceptLanguage to goi18n.NewLocalizer, read Accept-Language from the request without a size/shape bound, and globally registered the middleware. The underlying parser behavior pre-existed in dependencies, but Ech0's remotely reachable unbounded data path did not exist in the immediate parent.

audit_record.bug_semantics: File Browser authorized only the requested source root and, for copy or rename, the destination root, then recursively removed, renamed, or copied the whole source tree without checking rules on every descendant. An authenticated restricted user could therefore operate on an allowed parent containing a denied child, exposing or relocating the child at an allowed destination or deleting it with the parent.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit f6816c9a39702484ad7c5c3672209bbc4ce5f948 is the smallest reachable first-writer of the vulnerable resource operation: it created api.go, made serveAPI call c.us.Allowed only on r.URL.Path, routed DELETE to deleteHandler, and had deleteHandler recursively call c.us.fileSystem.RemoveAll on that root. Its immediate parent had no resource delete handler or equivalent user-filesystem recursive deletion. Commit 15f997faf0ff629d8da490c52c023e68a2eb7154 later added rename under the same root-only model, commit 05896697fa2730e59b8bcf6f1253da0f6fb8b5a9 later added copy while retaining only a root rule gate, and b4067cc423b1a0a9d24441bd52e2a53207a49fe9 merely split the already-vulnerable api.go handlers into resource.go rather than originating the flaw.

primary_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated non-administrator can select a directory whose root path is allowed even though a descendant is denied by a path rule. Copy, rename, and delete then recurse over the filesystem subtree without authorizing each source descendant and, for copy/rename, the corresponding destination descendant. The user can therefore expose or relocate denied content at an allowed destination, or destroy it by deleting its allowed parent.

Commit 05896697fa2730e59b8bcf6f1253da0f6fb8b5a9 later added only one c.User.Allowed(r.URL.Path) gate before dispatch, creating the root-authorized/descendants-unchecked form; commit 149465ab5278c135030466632c7fa79905c4646b added the copy variant. The v2 rewrite and later root checks preserved the same missing descendant authorization until the 2026 fix.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Access-rule authorization compared raw virtual paths as case-sensitive, slash-separated strings, while the host filesystem resolved equivalent names using its own case and separator semantics. On case-insensitive filesystems, a case variant of a denied path therefore missed the rule but reached the same file; on Windows, backslashes and traversal components likewise missed slash-based rules but were normalized by the filesystem. An authenticated user could consequently read or, subject to ordinary permissions, mutate an administrator-denied file while remaining inside the user's filesystem scope.

Its sole parent 780f1bc16e4e5270fed2a6b7da442a47084d8c4b has no Rule type, User.Allowed function, or vulnerable comparison. The earlier 20baeeb41a9555cefc3b31b495e24e907736c443 was a 10,626-line bulk import explicitly described as based on caddy-filemanager and was removed during the rewrite, so it is rejected as an import rather than selected as the BIC. Later commits moved or extracted the same mechanism, and public master received it in squash aggregate 12b2c215221696de58431093e01eeff7a5414471.

primary_record.bug_semantics: Access rules treated the request path as a case-sensitive, slash-separated string and performed literal/prefix matching before the same path was resolved by the host filesystem. On case-insensitive filesystems, a case variant of a denied path therefore missed the rule but named the denied file; on Windows, backslashes and traversal components likewise missed the rule but were normalized by the filesystem. An authenticated user could consequently disclose or mutate an administrator-denied file within the user's filesystem scope.
primary_record.flaw_origin: Commit 9c36dea485ddd16a90f0a615e20baddaee6b9cde first added the access-rule model and its vulnerable enforcement in one change: filemanager.go's User.Allowed compared the uncanonicalized URL with strings.HasPrefix(url, rule.Path), while newly added http.go passed raw request-derived paths to Allowed and then performed filesystem operations. Its immediate parent 780f1bc16e4e5270fed2a6b7da442a47084d8c4b contains none of Rule, User.Allowed, or that comparison. Later commits only moved, extracted, or broadened this mechanism, and the v2 rewrite aggregate preserved it.

review_record.bug_semantics: Authenticated users remain inside their configured filesystem scope but can bypass administrator path deny rules because authorization compares the uncanonicalized virtual path literally while the backing filesystem resolves an equivalent name differently. On case-insensitive filesystems, a case variant such as /secret.TXT names denied /Secret.txt without matching its case-sensitive rule. On Windows, a mixed-separator traversal such as /allow\..\Secret.txt likewise misses the slash-based rule while filepath/afero resolves it to the denied file. The affected operations include reads and, subject to the user's ordinary permissions, modification, deletion, copying, and sharing; internally generated OS-separated paths also caused nested recursive/archive checks to miss rules on Windows.
review_record.flaw_origin: The recoverable pre-squash PR history is two-stage. Commit 3dcbdfc8776b25f58a9134ba9f4d893f62db2b7c first wrote the flawed path-rule primitive: User.IsAllowed uses raw, case-sensitive strings.HasPrefix(url, rule.Path), while User.BuildFs exposes the scope through afero.NewBasePathFs and therefore host filesystem path semantics. Commit 41828f18050c3e90fc54ea2468324246b45e7d85 then activated that primitive at the HTTP resource gate and directory-listing checks. The smallest source-level flaw origin is 3dcbdfc8776b25f58a9134ba9f4d893f62db2b7c; later moves through types/rule.go, lib/rule.go, rules/rules.go, and master squash 12b2c215221696de58431093e01eeff7a5414471 preserve rather than originate it.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated BASIC app user can POST /api/attachments/:datasourceId/url because the route uses TABLE/WRITE authorization, which BASIC holds by default. getSignedUploadURL then loads the named S3 datasource's stored IAM credentials and signs PutObject for the request body's bucket and key. Normal S3 datasource configuration does not define a datasource-level bucket, so a BASIC user can obtain a presigned upload URL for any bucket writable by those credentials.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated user with Create permission could create a TUS upload with a small finite Upload-Length, then send a PATCH body larger than Upload-Length minus Upload-Offset. tusPatchHandler streamed the entire body to the file with io.Copy before comparing the resulting offset with the cached declared length; reaching or exceeding that length merely completed the upload. The excess bytes therefore remained on disk, and repeated oversized PATCH uploads could exhaust the filesystem.
audit_record.flaw_origin: PR #5270 member 6337c4452529dfc018885a7d05cc4f1e217316c5 first made FileBrowser accept and retain the client's finite Upload-Length: it added registerUpload/getActiveUploadLength, retrieved that value in tusPatchHandler, and used it only after the pre-existing unbounded io.Copy to unregister a completed upload. Its direct parent advertised Upload-Length: -1 and neither parsed nor tracked a declared length, so the advisory-specific promise-and-bypass mechanism did not yet exist. GitHub later squash-merged the PR as 0f27c91eca581482ce4f82f6429f5dac12f8b64e.

In tag v2.63.18, http/tus_handlers.go registers Upload-Length during POST, retrieves it during PATCH, performs bytesWritten, err := io.Copy(openFile, r.Body), and only afterwards computes newOffset and completes when newOffset >= uploadLength. git log -S over http/tus_handlers.go leads to squash 0f27c91eca581482ce4f82f6429f5dac12f8b64e. Direct-parent tree https://raw.githubusercontent.com/filebrowser/filebrowser/47b3e218ad7ffac4bc62294ec589a33ef3d4ea04/http/tus_handlers.go has no activeUploads, registerUpload, getActiveUploadLength, or getUploadLength; POST ignores Upload-Length and HEAD returns Upload-Length: -1, directly proving the finite-length bypass absent. Squash reconstruction is exact at the landing boundary: git show reports squash 0f27c91eca581482ce4f82f6429f5dac12f8b64e tree b0768b78cd59fcbb1ba36352faf6bd7bd6c13756, equal to PR head 40e184929ab0d8f73ed39f414942d4dfdb225427's tree from the PR API. Tag ancestry checks show v2.38.0 does not contain the squash, v2.39.0 does, v2.63.18 contains it, and v2.63.19 contains fix 4daddec6f200b03a721197d8c0b4b652c994894e plus regression commit 4c3cb4bc9b7a165ef42cf79f0e0842bbc42e26fd. The fix bounds copying with io.LimitReader(r.Body, remaining+1), rejects offset beyond declared length, truncates an over-length chunk, and returns 413.

Its security-relevant invariant began when FileBrowser accepted a finite TUS Upload-Length and represented that length as the accepted upload bound. The smallest causal commit is therefore decomposed member 6337c4452529dfc018885a7d05cc4f1e217316c5, not the 2023 commit that originally added an unbounded PATCH copier, not later ttlcache/refactor members, and not aggregate squash 0f27c91eca581482ce4f82f6429f5dac12f8b64e. review_record.bug_semantics: The authenticated TUS PATCH endpoint appended the entire request body with io.Copy even after the server had parsed and cached the Upload-Length declared at upload creation. The cached length was consulted only after the write to decide that an upload was complete. A create-capable user could therefore declare a 1 KiB upload and stream an arbitrarily large PATCH body, which was fully written before HTTP 204, allowing disk exhaustion. The fix bounds each write to Upload-Length minus Upload-Offset, rejects an already-excessive offset, and truncates and returns 413 when the body is over-length.
review_record.flaw_origin: The smallest causal commit is PR #5270 member 6337c4452529dfc018885a7d05cc4f1e217316c5, not its later GitHub squash 0f27c91eca581482ce4f82f6429f5dac12f8b64e and not the 2023 commit that originally added io.Copy. Member 6337c4452529dfc018885a7d05cc4f1e217316c5 first parsed Upload-Length, registered that accepted length, retrieved it in PATCH, and compared newOffset against it only after the pre-existing unbounded copy. Before that member, the endpoint had an unbounded upload operation but no accepted/cached per-upload declared bound; consistent with the first-party advisory's out-of-scope distinction for uploads without such a bound, that older behavior is not this specific bypass.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated user whose same-scope account has Perm.Download=false can call GET /api/resources/<path>?checksum=<md5|sha1|sha256|sha512>. resourceGetHandler invokes FileInfo.Checksum, which opens and reads the file, then serializes the digest, without first enforcing Perm.Download. The response is therefore a same-scope content-hash oracle that can confirm guessed content, reveal changes, and support offline brute force of low-entropy files; it does not bypass path/scope authorization.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The first reachable v2 implementation commit, 42227d9edd7ce613e8b6c0ad62c8cad16cf77266, added both the granular Download permission in types/user.go and the new http/resource.go checksum branch, but the branch checked no Download permission. The old immediate-parent model had no Download permission, so this member commit first created the relevant permission-bypass mechanism. Master later squashed PR #575 into 12b2c215221696de58431093e01eeff7a5414471. The 2026 commit 1e03feadb550e4414b5589a6a8df57f538efba15 fixed content-returning paths for CVE-2026-35606 but merely left the older checksum flaw in place; it did not write the vulnerable checksum lines.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the exact BIC commit object names Henrique Dias <hacdias@gmail.com> as both author and committer; its message has License: MIT and Signed-off-by: Henrique Dias <hacdias@gmail.com> trailers only, with no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI marker

Its b7dc392838f11d188f0bc0f2a1a99fad3f7dca03 reference is not a security change: git show identifies that object as an unrelated www/docs/installation.md PID-to-UID typo fix.

Aggregate 12b2c215221696de58431093e01eeff7a5414471 is titled 'feat: v2 (#599)' and explicitly points to PR #575, so it is not treated as the smallest BIC. The first PR #575 member is 42227d9edd7ce613e8b6c0ad62c8cad16cf77266. Its commit API diff reports http/resource.go and types/user.go as added relative to its sole parent c01ebf33efed835680373668e54d9ddafc90a6b1.

At 42227d9edd7ce613e8b6c0ad62c8cad16cf77266, http/resource.go lines 95-108 call file.Checksum(checksum) and clear file.Content without checking user.Perm.Download, while types/user.go line 27 declares Download bool. These two additions create the vulnerable authorization mismatch in one smallest reachable member commit.

Direct parent verification used the exact parent commit/tree objects: c01ebf33efed835680373668e54d9ddafc90a6b1 has tree ffa00c471a28cdb72ebf6e5dc46c57c945d241a4, whose root contains neither http nor types; the BIC diff marks both vulnerable files added. The parent's lib/filebrowser.go User fields are AllowCommands, AllowEdit, AllowNew, and AllowPublish and contain no Download permission. Thus the combined Download-permission/checksum-bypass mechanism is absent from the immediate parent.

Version-boundary checks show 12b2c215221696de58431093e01eeff7a5414471 is an ancestor of v2.0.0. git grep at v2.0.0 finds the unguarded checksum branch at http/resource.go:36, the Download permission at users/permissions.go:12, and a contrasting Download guard at http/raw.go:60, proving the flaw was present at the first v2 release boundary.

Commit 1e03feadb550e4414b5589a6a8df57f538efba15 ('fix: check download permission in resource handler') changed FileOptions.Content to d.user.Perm.Download and guarded the X-Encoding path, but did not modify the checksum branch. This explains why CVE-2026-72834 is a residual/incomplete-fix issue without making 1e03feadb550e4414b5589a6a8df57f538efba15 the BIC.

Direct fix 6c69b5cd895e15b29e563200a9a6dfc27b06525e adds if !d.user.Perm.Download { return http.StatusAccepted, nil } immediately before file.Checksum in http/resource.go. git merge-base --is-ancestor returns false for this fix against v2.63.18 and true against v2.63.19; the repository changelog names the same commit as 'enforce download permission on the checksum branch'.

audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerable behavior is the checksum branch's full-file read and digest disclosure under a user model that separately denies downloads. audit_record.bug_semantics: On a fresh instance with no password configured, check_auth() deliberately admitted every request. POST /api/settings nevertheless accepted the ownership-establishing _set_password pseudo-setting: save_settings() hashed the attacker-chosen value into settings.json as password_hash, turning authentication on. A remote unauthenticated first caller could therefore choose the initial credential, authenticate (and, after the later session-continuity change, receive a session immediately), and lock out the intended operator. The missing invariant was that the unauthenticated disabled-auth state must not permit a non-local client to perform the transition that establishes the first trust root.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The optional-password feature commit introduced both halves of the flaw together: api/auth.py made check_auth() return true whenever no password existed, while api/config.py made the already-generic /api/settings save path interpret untrusted _set_password as authority to persist the first password. It added no locality, bootstrap token, or existing-owner check around that transition. A later commit only added automatic cookie issuance; it did not originate the takeover because an attacker could already log in with the password they selected.

review_record.bug_semantics: When no password was configured, check_auth deliberately authorized every request, including POST /api/settings. The settings writer nevertheless accepted the private _set_password field, hashed it into persistent password_hash, and thereby enabled authentication with an attacker-chosen password. A remote unauthenticated client reaching the WebUI during first run could therefore claim ownership, then authenticate with that password; from 8b857d9efc121586f2ef79ca4b8f92d8ad373b5b onward the same bootstrap response also created and returned a valid session cookie immediately.
review_record.flaw_origin: b8b62722ec2f6b3cd394737ab409c35650f29ca6 introduced the complete unsafe bootstrap primitive in one ordinary commit: api/auth.py made all routes pass while auth was disabled and exposed public password login, server.py applied that middleware, and api/config.py made save_settings consume _set_password and persist password_hash without a local-origin gate. The pre-existing generic POST /api/settings route supplied the remotely reachable sink.

`git show b8b62722ec2f6b3cd394737ab409c35650f29ca6 -- api/config.py api/auth.py api/routes.py server.py` shows the causal chain: save_settings accepts _set_password and stores its hash; new check_auth returns True whenever is_auth_enabled() is false; server.py invokes check_auth before POST dispatch; and /api/auth/login verifies the chosen password and calls create_session. The original disclosure at https://github.com/itsnishat08/CVE-2025-63700 only describes changing one authentication strategy to another and alleged backend non-revalidation; it provides no endpoint transcript, strategy values, PoC, patch, or commit. Version check: git rev-parse @clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0^{} resolves the affected tag to c3facf1d1877261c01be5a446458f37e75c6d354 (tagged 2025-08-21); GitHub still lists <=5.88.0 and 'Patched versions: None'. Source check at that tag: packages/clerk-js/src/core/resources/SignIn.ts attemptFirstFactor and attemptSecondFactor post the supplied body to attempt_first_factor/attempt_second_factor and therefore delegate validation to FAPI. History check: blame leads those generic posting lines to 8b00a66c18924a2a99afdb3539bd6663d68eb673, 'More Clerk packages going Open Source (#20)', a 2,093-line wholesale package import. Its immediate parent 679ab0e0054250cf9269d28b097cac043ac761a1 has only backend-core, edge, and sdk-node under packages and no clerk-js tree. That aggregate is not a smallest BIC and cannot be decomposed from this public history. No fix commit or patched release exists because the issue was withdrawn as non-security; the post-boundary @clerk/clerk-js@5.89.0 tag resolves to 3cb634c4a9431a4680350351ffc1516b99e4157e, and its intervening OTP commit f871573b5546a27719a2e8f3e5529594db8828bc only rewrites the visual OTP input for autofill/password-manager compatibility, not server verification.
primary_record.reasoning: Vulnerability-first reconstruction stops before AI attribution. The only described attack requires a server to accept a manipulated verification strategy without validating it against the prepared sign-in state. The JavaScript SDK merely serializes and sends that request, so its generic attempt-factor methods are not the authorization root cause. More decisively, the canonical CNA later withdrew CVE-2025-63700 after determining that it was not a security issue. Consequently there are no proven vulnerable lines, no real BIC whose parent can demonstrate flaw absence, and no security fix or patched boundary to identify. The oldest public client transport code is a wholesale open-source import rather than an atomic introducer, and treating it as the BIC would violate the smallest-BIC rule. With no BIC, inspecting that aggregate's authorship or trailers would also violate BIC-only AI attribution. A closed NOT_AI or AI verdict is therefore unsupported; EVIDENCE_GAP records that the stale GHSA/bundle claim cannot be mapped to a valid vulnerability lifecycle.
primary_record.remaining_gap: No valid vulnerability mechanism, smallest BIC, parent-absence proof, or fix exists to audit: the CNA rejected CVE-2025-63700 as not a security issue, while GitHub's GHSA page remains stale. Reopening attribution would require a reproducible request/response transcript proving the claimed bypass and access to the causal FAPI server implementation/history; absent that, no BIC-only AI verdict is possible.

review_record.bug_semantics: The withdrawn report alleged that, after beginning an OAuth sign-in and reaching an OTP challenge, an attacker could alter the attempt request's authentication strategy (for example, swap an email-code attempt to another factor) and have the server complete authentication without the correct code. The public clerk-js 5.88.0 UI does send the factor strategy and entered code to the Frontend API, but that client-controlled request is not an authentication trust boundary; the alleged bypass requires the server to accept a strategy that was not valid for the sign-in attempt. The CNA later rejected CVE-2025-63700 because further investigation established that this was not a security issue.
review_record.flaw_origin: No verified flaw exists in the audited repository. The allegation depended on improper state/factor validation by Clerk's non-public Frontend API backend, while clerk/javascript only constructs and sends the client request. The relevant client request behavior predates 5.88.0 and was unchanged by that release, and the authoritative CVE record plus Clerk's first-party vulnerability history state that the report was investigated, withdrawn, and never a real vulnerability.
review_record.ai_marker: unverified — BIC commit-object AI marker could not be established; see remaining_gap
evidence: Authoritative lifecycle: fetch https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/CVE-2025-63700 and inspect cveMetadata plus containers.cna.rejectedReasons. The record is state REJECTED, dateRejected 2025-12-23, and says: 'Further investigation showed that it was not a security issue.' NVD's https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-63700 reports the same Rejected status and reason.

First-party disposition: in https://clerk.com/articles/clerk-security-how-we-protect-your-users, section 'Subsequent disclosures, 2025 to 2026', Clerk states that CVE-2025-63700 was a disputed external report, was rejected as 'not a security issue', and 'was never a real vulnerability.' Original advisory boundary: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3mm3-wfpv-q85g records @clerk/clerk-js <= 5.88.0, 'Patched versions: None', publication 2025-11-20, and update 2025-11-21. The bundle likewise has first_patched_version null. This predates the CNA's 2025-12-23 rejection and explains why the stale GHSA still describes the allegation without a patch.

Release boundary in the clone: `git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short) %(objectname) %(*objectname) %(*authordate:iso-strict)' refs/tags/@clerk/clerk-js@5.87.0 refs/tags/@clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0 refs/tags/@clerk/clerk-js@5.89.0` peels the release tags to 6a1fb13a389b2b97db286539f0e9a7ef018ea5ab (5.87.0), c3facf1d1877261c01be5a446458f37e75c6d354 (5.88.0, 2025-08-21), and 3cb634c4a9431a4680350351ffc1516b99e4157e (5.89.0, 2025-08-26). `git show @clerk/clerk-js@5.89.0:packages/clerk-js/CHANGELOG.md` contains no security fix for this allegation; its OTP change is an input-widget rework.

No 5.88 BIC: `git diff --name-status @clerk/clerk-js@5.87.0 @clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0 -- packages/clerk-js/src/core/resources/SignIn.ts packages/clerk-js/src/ui/components/SignIn` shows no change to SignIn.ts; only SignInAccountSwitcher.tsx and SignIn/index.tsx changed, both for unrelated session-task navigation. `git diff @clerk/clerk-js@5.87.0 @clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0 -- packages/clerk-js/CHANGELOG.md` lists captcha, an OAuth immediate-redirect allowlist entry, billing, session-task routing, passkey visibility, and navigation changes, not OTP verification acceptance.

Client-path reconstruction: `git show @clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0:packages/clerk-js/src/ui/components/SignIn/SignInFactorOneCodeForm.tsx` shows the UI calling `attemptFirstFactor({ strategy: props.factor.strategy, code })`; `git show @clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0:packages/clerk-js/src/core/resources/SignIn.ts` shows attemptFirstFactor posting those parameters to action `attempt_first_factor`. This proves only that the browser identifies the attempted factor, not that the server accepts a mismatched or unprepared factor.

History cross-check: `git log -L 182,199:packages/clerk-js/src/core/resources/SignIn.ts @clerk/clerk-js@5.88.0` traces the generic attempt_first_factor POST through 2024/2023/2022 and back to the public-source import 8b00a66c18924a2a99afdb3539bd6663d68eb673 (parent 679ab0e0054250cf9269d28b097cac043ac761a1) on 2022-02-04. That commit is not selected as a BIC because the CNA/vendor evidence establishes that the request construction is not a vulnerability. With no true BIC, direct parent absence and BIC commit-object AI attribution cannot truthfully be asserted.
review_record.reasoning: The report's proposed attack crosses the browser/server boundary: changing a browser request is always possible, so a bypass exists only if the Frontend API fails to bind an OTP attempt to the prepared factor and sign-in state. The public SDK at 5.88.0 passes the UI-selected factor strategy and code to that API, but contains no server-side authentication decision. Git diff shows 5.88.0 did not introduce the relevant request path, and git log -L shows the generic path existed years earlier. There is no closing patch or first patched package version; 5.89.0's OTP work only changes the input UI. Most decisively, on 2025-12-23 the CNA withdrew the CVE after determining it was not a security issue, and Clerk's first-party history says it was never a real vulnerability. Selecting the 2022 request helper, the 5.88.0 release commit, or any later change as a BIC would therefore violate the protocol's requirement for the smallest commit that first wrote genuinely vulnerable lines. Since no true BIC exists, there is no parent-absence claim and no BIC commit object on which an AI marker may be judged. EVIDENCE_GAP is used rather than NOT_AI because a closed NOT_AI verdict requires a real BIC; it is used rather than BLOCKED because the repository and public lifecycle are accessible, but the reachable evidence does not establish any vulnerability to attribute.
review_record.remaining_gap: A closed AI/non-AI attribution would require a reproducible authentication bypass plus the actual code and history of the server-side factor/state validation that caused and fixed it. No such reproducer, vulnerable backend line, fix commit, or patched version is present in the cited report or public repository, and the CNA/vendor instead affirmatively concluded that the report was not a security issue. Consequently there is no defensible BIC, parent-absence proof, fix SHA, or BIC-only AI marker to record.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The standard HR employee-create form collected an email and employee details but no password, while EmployeeSaveController::save() assigned bcrypt($request->input('password', 'changeme')). Consequently, every employee created through that product flow received the same predictable literal credential. The created record was App\Models\User, an Illuminate Authenticatable model used by the normal login path, so a remote attacker who knew an onboarded employee's email could log in as that employee with changeme; no first-login change or reset step invalidated the credential.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The smallest first-writer is decomposed pull-request member 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6. It created EmployeeSaveController with the changeme fallback, created the shared passwordless employee form, registered POST /rrhh/employee/save, and advanced APP_VERSION from 5.9.2 to 5.10.0. GitHub squash 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64 aggregated that member and 8369823e08d5ce346527ae6950a588619f821bc6; the latter changed only routes/module/payroll.php, so the aggregate is not the smallest BIC.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the complete commit object for BIC 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 names human author and committer Gustavo Novaro <gnovaro@gmail.com> and its message has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, AI-tool, or bot trailer/marker
audit_record.evidence: First-party Secur0 advisory https://secur0.com/en/cna/cve-list/cve-2026-19871-hardcoded-credentials-in-prospero-flow-crm-employee-onboarding identifies EmployeeSaveController, the passwordless shared form, affected versions beginning with the module at 5.10.0 and before 5.15.9, vulnerable tag v5.14.0, and advisory fix https://github.com/Roskus/prospero-flow-crm/commit/5cc01ed958db4ad0a026a8daa1c6a8bb98a43e66. `git log -L '/validated.*password/,+1':app/Http/Controllers/Rrhh/Employee/EmployeeSaveController.php 5cc01ed9...` traces the exact line from its creation as `$validated['password'] = bcrypt($request->input('password', 'changeme'));` in mainline squash 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64 to replacement by `bcrypt(Str::random(32))` in 5cc01ed958db4ad0a026a8daa1c6a8bb98a43e66; `git log --all -S"'changeme'" -- <controller>` returns only those introduction/removal mainline commits. GitHub API `GET /repos/Roskus/prospero-flow-crm/pulls/258/commits` reconstructs members 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 (parent 9e4f84ece7e13c2c327540804dcaf841c6ac23fa) and 8369823e08d5ce346527ae6950a588619f821bc6; `git show 33a30a5d...` proves the first member created the controller, passwordless `_form.blade.php`, RRHH route, and version 5.10.0, while `git show 8369823e...` proves the second touched only the payroll update route. The final member tree a74da6513163046124c133789294353d268087bd equals squash 04d1afd7's tree, proving incorporation. Direct parent verification with `git ls-tree -r --name-only 9e4f84ece7e13c2c327540804dcaf841c6ac23fa -- app/Http/Controllers/Rrhh/Employee/EmployeeSaveController.php resources/views/rrhh/employee/_form.blade.php routes/module/rrhh.php` produced no paths: the controller, form, route, and vulnerable assignment were absent. At the BIC, `app/Models/User.php` extends Illuminate's Authenticatable and accepts password in `$fillable`; the form contains no password input. MainController has auth middleware for the staff onboarding operation, but the resulting employee User credential is usable by an otherwise unauthenticated attacker at the normal login. Version checks: the BIC changes version.php from 5.9.2 to 5.10.0; `git tag --contains 04d1afd7...` returns v5.14.0 and `git show v5.14.0:version.php` says 5.14.0, while that tag still has changeme. `git show 5cc01ed9...:version.php` says 5.15.9 and `git tag --contains 5cc01ed9...` returns no tag, matching the advisory's statement that the fix is not yet tagged. `git show c58853a4e3d4cdb554955363a8d0ea8946c869e8 -- <controller>` shows the first direct PR #263 member removing changeme for a random temporary password; the final squash further uses a 32-byte random password, sets must_change_password, assigns the User role, and sends a password-reset link. GitHub PR #263 commit API links c58853a4e3d4cdb554955363a8d0ea8946c869e8 to the fix series, and the final PR-member tree 9e51bc96e7e3cab0302b773b88fa32529a84042c equals the 5cc01ed9 squash tree. Finally, `git cat-file -p 33a30a5d...` is the BIC-only AI check: human author/committer Gustavo Novaro and no trailers or AI marker.
audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerable lifecycle begins atomically in PR #258's first member: the controller hard-codes a default credential at the same time the only standard onboarding form omits a password and the route/model make a real login-capable User. Its immediate parent has none of those HR files, so this is creation rather than a move or refactor. The public mainline squash is one commit later only in representation: the PR API preserves the two member objects, the first member contains every causal line, the second is an unrelated payroll-route correction, and the aggregate tree matches the final member tree. Thus 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 is smaller than 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64 and is the real BIC. The module entered at 5.10.0, remained present in tagged 5.14.0, and was removed at the repository's 5.15.9 commit. Fix member c58853a4e3d4cdb554955363a8d0ea8946c869e8 first eliminates the shared literal; advisory fix squash 5cc01ed958db4ad0a026a8daa1c6a8bb98a43e66 lands the final random-password/reset-link/forced-change design. Attribution is judged only from the decomposed BIC commit object, not the squash, PR text, or fix: it contains a human author and committer and no AI marker. Therefore the closed causal verdict is NOT_AI.

review_record.bug_semantics: The standard HR employee-creation flow at POST /rrhh/employee/save accepted an email address but exposed and validated no password field. EmployeeSaveController nevertheless created the application's normal Authenticatable User record with bcrypt($request->input('password', 'changeme')); because the bundled form could not submit a password, every normally onboarded employee received the predictable password changeme. An unauthenticated remote attacker who knew an onboarded employee's email address could therefore use the ordinary email/password login and obtain that employee account's reachable data and actions.
review_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable HR module was squash-merged to main as 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64 (PR #258), but that aggregate is not the smallest BIC. The PR patch decomposes into 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 followed by 8369823e08d5ce346527ae6950a588619f821bc6. Atomic member 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 first added EmployeeSaveController with the changeme fallback, the password-less employee form, and the save route; 8369823e08d5ce346527ae6950a588619f821bc6 only added a missing payroll update route.
review_record.ai_marker: Absent on the BIC commit object. `git cat-file -p 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6` shows author and committer Gustavo Novaro <gnovaro@gmail.com> and only the subject `feat: New RRHH module with employee management, time tracking, payroll, and company holiday calendar`; there is no Co-authored-by, Generated-with, or other AI attribution trailer, and neither identity is a bot.
review_record.evidence: In the validated clone, `git log 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 --reverse -S'bcrypt($request->input('password', 'changeme'))' -- app/Http/Controllers/Rrhh/Employee/EmployeeSaveController.php` resolves the first writer to 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6, and `git log -L 27,30:app/Http/Controllers/Rrhh/Employee/EmployeeSaveController.php 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6` shows that exact assignment added from /dev/null. `git ls-tree -r --name-only 9e4f84ece7e13c2c327540804dcaf841c6ac23fa -- app/Http/Controllers/Rrhh/Employee/EmployeeSaveController.php resources/views/rrhh/employee/_form.blade.php routes/module/rrhh.php` returns no paths, while the parent-to-BIC diff reports all three as added, directly proving parent absence. The first-party PR #258 patch names members 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6 and 8369823e08d5ce346527ae6950a588619f821bc6; `git rev-parse 8369823e08d5ce346527ae6950a588619f821bc6^{tree} 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64^{tree}` returns the same tree a74da6513163046124c133789294353d268087bd for the final member and squash merge. At the BIC, EmployeeSaveController extends MainController (whose middleware includes auth and locked), POST /rrhh/employee/save invokes save(), the employee form has email but no password input, User extends Authenticatable with email and password fillable, and the guest LoginController uses Laravel's AuthenticatesUsers with the normal email/password form. `version.php` is 5.9.2 in the parent and 5.10.0 in the BIC. The main-history squash 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64 is contained by tag v5.14.0, whose version.php says 5.14.0, proving a tagged vulnerable release; the fix parent e0f3111185035179a0453a717cf67bf9a0eba572 says 5.14.3. The first-party advisory states affected before 5.15.9. PR #263 member c58853a4e3d4cdb554955363a8d0ea8946c869e8 directly removes the changeme assignment and uses a random 16-character password; the squash fix 5cc01ed958db4ad0a026a8daa1c6a8bb98a43e66 contains the final stronger flow (random 32-character password, must-change flag, reset link) and changes version.php to 5.15.9. `git tag --contains 5cc01ed958db4ad0a026a8daa1c6a8bb98a43e66` is empty, so no repository tag contains the fix; `git tag --contains 04d1afd73226b1572fd19dc5ee5bbb55b82a1a64` returns v5.14.0. Existing accounts created with changeme remain weak until their passwords are reset, as the first-party solution notes.
review_record.reasoning: The vulnerability requires the combination written atomically by PR member 33a30a5d0de8714198b063742405aa82ae9abda6: a predictable literal fallback, a standard form unable to override it, creation of the same User model accepted by the public login, and a reachable employee save route for normal onboarding. Its immediate parent lacks the HR controller, form, and route, so this is the smallest true BIC rather than the later squash aggregate. The direct fix member c58853a4e3d4cdb554955363a8d0ea8946c869e8 first eliminates the shared credential; the published main-history fix 5cc01ed958db4ad0a026a8daa1c6a8bb98a43e66 lands the final reset-link design at 5.15.9. AI judgment is restricted to the BIC object: it has a human author/committer and no AI attribution marker, so the causal verdict is NOT_AI regardless of bot-authored PR commentary or later commits.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated caller can send PUT /api/supplier/{id} with another tenant's supplier ID. SupplierRequest::authorize() checks only Auth::check(), SupplierUpdateController resolves the attacker-controlled ID globally with Supplier::find($id), and update($request->all()) mass-assigns body fields against Supplier::$fillable, which includes company_id. The caller can therefore read and modify the returned foreign supplier and can reassign it by supplying company_id.

audit_record.bug_semantics: A logged-in user could submit a saved graph configuration whose config_json was checked only for syntactically valid JSON. The server stored and returned the object without a property allowlist; an administrator's list included every user's saved configurations. Loading one parsed the stored JSON and applyConfig spread every property of attacker-controlled stixStyles or mispStyles entries into GRAPH_CONFIG. Those style maps were then passed to Pivotick as nodeStyleMap/defaultNodeStyle, and Pivotick interpreted a supplied svgIcon as HTML, so viewing/loading the saved configuration could execute attacker script in another user's browser.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit a0a9834b21b40ab570db54e1c6e6c2cf100b5f9a introduced the complete unsafe saved-configuration path in one focused feature commit: the graph_config model and save/list routes, unrestricted JSON persistence, the saved-config loader, and applyConfig's unrestricted style-object spreads. Its immediate parent had none of the graph-config persistence, loading, or patch-application mechanism, making this ordinary one-parent feature commit the smallest reconstructable BIC rather than the later branch merge or a release commit.

review_record.bug_semantics: Stored graph-configuration XSS. An authenticated low-privilege user could POST a config_json object containing a style such as mispStyles.Event.svgIcon. The save route checked only that the string parsed as JSON and persisted the complete object; the list route returned the stored string unchanged. When a viewer with access to the saved row (notably an administrator, because administrators list every user's configs) loaded it, graphConfigModal.js parsed config_json and applyConfig() spread every property of each stixStyles/mispStyles entry into GRAPH_CONFIG. A subsequent graph render passed that style map to Pivotick as nodeStyleMap. The bundled Pivotick renderer treats svgIcon as markup (both a template path using template.innerHTML = i.svgIcon.trim() and node rendering using an SVG element's innerHTML), so a crafted SVG event handler executes in the viewer's browser. Loading/applying the saved configuration is the victim interaction.
review_record.flaw_origin: Commit a0a9834b21b40ab570db54e1c6e6c2cf100b5f9a is the atomic first writer of the vulnerable cross-user path. It added the GraphConfig table/model, /graph_config/save and /graph_config/list, the saved-config modal/load code, and applyConfig(), whose unrestricted object spread copied attacker-controlled style members such as svgIcon into GRAPH_CONFIG. The pre-existing parent already rendered trusted built-in styles with Pivotick, but had no saved-config file, persistence route, load path, or applyConfig bridge from another user's stored JSON to that renderer.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Authenticated ticket routes accepted a user-controlled numeric ticket id without constraining the selected Ticket to the authenticated user's company_id. GET /ticket/update/{id} exposed another tenant's ticket content and, once attachment support existed, its attachments; POST /ticket/save loaded another tenant's Ticket and then reassigned company_id and saved it; GET /ticket/delete/{id} deleted an arbitrary Ticket while its generic Request type also bypassed TicketDeleteRequest authorization.

Commit 65f6b9f961efe533b4d3f20f1eddad132fe8ef1d merely moved the already-vulnerable save lookup into TicketRepository and is not an introducer.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The conversion-history details endpoint reads a ConversionHistory row by caller-supplied history_id and serializes retained input_text, old_output_text, and new_output_text. Once ordinary conversion deletion became a soft delete, the parent conversion and its history remained in the database. The later normal parent lookup hid inactive conversions and returned None, while the authorization guard denied only when the parent was truthy and invisible; a deleted parent therefore skipped denial and its history payload was returned. The endpoint was anonymous immediately after the soft-delete change and remained exploitable by authenticated requesters after the later login hardening.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit bf868699adf960e7f812d30ccc3f1fa28131ba34 is the smallest causal BIC. audit_record.bug_semantics: The authenticated POST /company/save path accepted a company-logo upload without any server-side type, extension, content, or size validation, derived the stored suffix from UploadedFile::extension(), and wrote the bytes into a web-public location. review_record.bug_semantics: POST /company/save accepted a company logo without server-side type, extension, size, or SVG-content validation. An authenticated user satisfying the route's create company and update company permission gates could upload an SVG containing an embedded script; the controller derived a .svg destination name and wrote it to public storage. The resulting /storage/company/{slug}/{file} resource was served statically outside Laravel authentication, so direct navigation by any visitor executed attacker-controlled JavaScript in the application origin.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The authenticated POST /contact/save path trusted the request's numeric contact id and loaded Contact::find(...) without company_id scoping before overwriting the record, so a user could blindly modify another tenant's contact. The authenticated GET /contact/export-vcard/{id} path likewise used Contact::findOrFail($id) without company_id scoping and returned the selected record's vCard, allowing cross-tenant PII disclosure by id enumeration.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The write primitive originated in 266c2bec31a4ef56431f0ee9ed4dfadfa12661b9, which added the authenticated /contact/save route and a new ContactSaveController whose update branch selected a Contact solely by attacker-controlled id; contacts were already owned through company-scoped leads, so the missing ownership check was exploitable at introduction. Commit 9fda3ee70b7b6035f729a154f7bf50bfabbd3b7f later added an explicit contact.company_id on creation while retaining the unscoped update. Commit 65f6b9f961efe533b4d3f20f1eddad132fe8ef1d merely moved the same vulnerable save logic into ContactRepository and is not the BIC. The independent vCard disclosure surface was added from scratch by a0306e77f95aaf57afec25ef74e4aa2da275c830.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Remote-data DOM XSS in the MISP event browser: the server accepts an operator-selected remote MISP instance, copies that instance's event fields into JSON, and the browser interpolates those values into template strings assigned to innerHTML. A malicious or compromised remote MISP can therefore inject markup or script-capable content through event IDs, information, organization/date/count/threat fields, tag names and colors, TLP/distribution labels, or flash/error text; unvalidated tag colors also enter inline CSS.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit b9f40af30de83fa44a14a3b0263df26192696b48 added the remote-MISP connection/browser feature and, in the same atomic commit, passed remote response fields through website/web/convert/convert.py and rendered them with div.innerHTML, overlay.innerHTML, and tr.innerHTML in website/web/templates/convert/misp_to_stix.html. The core mistake was treating remote-derived strings and colors as trusted HTML/CSS instead of creating DOM nodes and assigning textContent plus validating colors. Commit 26ecb7e6a608b5be73fa552928e00bef7cac4f22 later expanded selection/distribution behavior and added further instances of the same mechanism, but b9f40af30de83fa44a14a3b0263df26192696b48 is the earliest and smallest real BIC for the vulnerable event-browser mechanism.

The BIC's backend requests /events/index, parses the remote JSON, and returns selected fields essentially verbatim; the BIC's frontend then embeds those fields into HTML strings assigned to innerHTML. Finally, attribution is based only on the BIC commit object: it has a human author/committer and no AI marker or trailer. Under the protocol, that makes the closed verdict NOT_AI regardless of AI signals on unrelated commits.

review_record.bug_semantics: The MISP-to-STIX page lets an operator connect cti-transmute to a remote MISP server. The server-side /misp_search_events proxy copied remote event id, info, date, organization, attribute count, threat level, tag name, and tag colour into JSON, after which the browser interpolated those values into tr.innerHTML, tag/TLP badge HTML, distribution-label HTML, and flash HTML. A malicious or compromised remote MISP instance could therefore return crafted markup or script-capable attributes that execute in the cti-transmute origin when the operator browses or imports events; unvalidated remote tag colours also reached CSS background values.

audit_record.bug_semantics: rConfig deliberately disabled Laravel self-registration with Auth::routes(['register' => false]), but a later bare Auth::routes() call registered the framework's default registration endpoints again. An unauthenticated POST /register therefore reached RegisterController, whose create() method omitted role; the users.role database column defaulted to Admin, and the RegistersUsers flow authenticated the newly created account. The attacker consequently obtained a logged-in Administrator account without invitation, approval, or prior credentials.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The smallest first-writer is 5ae01b3781de867baad1a8aa8aebfc3448812f68. In the multiple-SSO feature commit, routes/web.php gained the single causally decisive line Auth::routes(); between the new SAML logout and provider redirect routes. The already-present disabled-registration call, framework registration controller, and Admin column default made that new route dangerous, but they did not expose registration while the only auth route declaration had register=false. The candidate's immediate parent 6202a5d9e061fce98de25ec8b62a4973c0dffd35 has no bare call.

The Claude co-author trailer on the later fix d3fe04fc9d2e1f892b9e21f037e4104badd565e3 is not evidence about the BIC.

The assigned global advisory https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-3xhw-7rxv-vwc7 / CVE-2026-77915 describes the same mechanism but its prose says before 8.2.13; repository history and the first-party advisory establish the actual 8.2.10 patch boundary. `git log -L 19,19:routes/web.php 5ae01b...` returns only 5ae01b3781de867baad1a8aa8aebfc3448812f68 and the hunk `@@ -11,0 +19,1 @@` / `+Auth::routes();`. `git ls-tree` plus `git cat-file -p` shows candidate blob 59bea0ad016c9dba5b26460ffeed896632f72edf contains both Auth::routes(['register' => false]) and the later Auth::routes(), while immediate-parent blob d374100b5aabd44348863b59163011513f7f8529 contains only the disabled-registration declaration; this directly verifies parent absence. audit_record.reasoning: The lifecycle is closed from introduction through release and repair. Registration was intentionally disabled before the BIC. Commit 5ae01b... added a second, unqualified Laravel auth-route declaration while implementing SSO; Laravel registers rather than retracts the default endpoints, so the new declaration reopened POST /register. This is smaller and more causal than treating the older controller/default or any later move/refactor/release commit as the BIC. Tag ancestry and route blobs place the flaw in the first 8.x release and through core-8.2.9, while d3fe04f... removes it in core-8.2.10; this concrete boundary resolves the later global advisory's imprecise 'before 8.2.13' wording in favor of first-party and repository evidence. Finally, only the BIC commit object controls attribution: it is authored and committed by danielrConfig and has no AI marker. The AI co-author trailer on the fix cannot retroactively attribute the BIC, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated GET /download-export request supplied filename directly to download_export(), which concatenated export_path() with the raw $_GET['filename'] value and, after only file_exists(), passed the resulting path to response()->download(). A filename containing ../ could therefore escape the exports directory and disclose any file readable by the web-server account.

audit_record.bug_semantics: In authenticated HTTP mode, an attacker-controlled Bearer token was treated as a session-file basename without restricting its alphabet or confining the resulting path. review_record.bug_semantics: In HTTP-auth mode, an unauthenticated client-controlled Bearer token was used as a filesystem path component. Existence/authorization of that legacy session therefore authenticated the attacker without a generated bearer secret; downstream account-prefixing did not restore the lost authentication boundary.

audit_record.bug_semantics: When the experimental Extension backend handles another node's added or removed lease, it JSON-unmarshals attacker-controlled flannel.alpha.coreos.com/backend-data and writes that string to stdin of runCmd while launching the configured SubnetAddCommand or SubnetRemoveCommand through sh -c. review_record.bug_semantics: LocalFolderExtractor canonicalized each attacker-controlled RAR entry path, but createDirectory() and createFile() decided containment with String.startsWith(destinationCanonicalPath). audit_record.bug_semantics: awxkit's custom PyYAML Loader registers !include and !import and sends attacker-controlled scalar, sequence, or mapping values to extractFile(). Before the fix, extractFile() joined those values to the importing stream's directory, expanded them with glob.glob(), converted matches to absolute paths, and opened and recursively parsed them without rejecting absolute paths, '..' traversal, or symlink escapes. A victim who runs 'awx --conf.format yaml import' on crafted YAML can therefore disclose arbitrary locally readable YAML-formatted files; this is a client-side confidentiality flaw requiring user interaction.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable Loader/extractFile code first appears in ansible/awx public history in 9616cc6f7856523ebf6d1580443313296c9f6507, but that commit is explicitly titled 'import awxkit' and adds 101 files with 10,479 lines. Its direct parent lacks awxkit/awxkit/yaml_file.py, and the associated two-commit range contains only that import plus an awxkit CI follow-up. It is therefore an aggregate public-history gateway for pre-existing awxkit/towerkit code, not the smallest commit that authored the flaw. The pre-import authoring history is unavailable, so the protocol-valid BIC cannot be named.

primary_record.bug_semantics: The awx CLI import command parses attacker-supplied YAML from client.stdin with awxkit.yaml_file.Loader. Loader registers !include and !import, and extractFile joins the directive value to the input stream's directory (which is empty for <stdin>), expands the result with glob.glob, converts matches to absolute paths, and opens and recursively parses them without rejecting absolute paths, '..' traversal, or symlink escapes. A user who imports a malicious YAML document can therefore disclose arbitrary locally readable YAML-formatted files.

Commit 405c56e2bcaee1965a6f57520623cfa47612c9e2 directly closes every relevant escape class and is therefore both the lifecycle fix and direct fix. History and tags establish that the unsafe component was publicly present from the 2019 awxkit import through the last affected 24.6.1 release, while the fix remains untagged. The only public first-hit commit is demonstrably a wholesale open-sourcing import, and neither its parent nor PR members preserve the earlier component history. Consequently the true smallest commit, its immediate parent, and its commit-object AI signals cannot be inspected. The boundary commit's human-only object cannot support NOT_AI for code it merely aggregated, so the correct verdict is BLOCKED rather than a fabricated closed attribution.

review_record.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /tokenTransfer/:token handler treats knowledge of a random transfer UUID as sufficient authority. audit_record.bug_semantics: On Linux/Unix, LocalFolderExtractor first constructs and canonicalizes new File(destination, archiveEntryName) while backslashes in the untrusted RAR name are still literal filename characters. A name such as '..\..\tmp\evil' therefore passes the destination-prefix check. If the file does not exist, makeFile then splits that same name on backslashes and rejoins the components with File.separator, turning the previously literal '..' components into real '/' traversal. extract subsequently opens FileOutputStream on that reconstructed path and writes attacker-controlled archive content outside the extraction directory.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The causal flaw is the two-stage, inconsistent interpretation of an archive pathname: validation and use do not operate on the same normalized representation. The backslash-splitting/reconstruction and write path first appear in the repository's root initial-import commit 6f32323c983015d96c64084418793853f514b519 in testutil/src/main/java/de/innosystec/unrar/testutil/ExtractArchive.java. review_record.bug_semantics: On Linux/Unix, an attacker-controlled RAR entry such as `..\..\tmp\evil.txt` is first checked as a child of the extraction directory while backslashes are literal filename characters, so `getCanonicalPath().startsWith(destination.getCanonicalPath())` accepts it. `makeFile()` then splits that same name on backslashes, joins the components with the platform `File.separator` (`/`), creates the resulting directories/file, and `extract()` writes attacker-controlled entry bytes through `FileOutputStream`. The validation and the write therefore interpret the same pathname differently, enabling traversal and arbitrary file overwrite outside the destination. Windows is not affected by this bypass because canonicalization already treats backslashes as separators.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Etherpad generated import/export working-file names in the shared process temporary directory from Math.random(), then used ordinary write, rename, and converter operations that follow existing symbolic links. A local low-privilege user who can predict a token and pre-create the corresponding /tmp path as a symlink can redirect Etherpad's file operation to a target writable by the Etherpad process, causing disclosure or overwrite; import output can contain attacker-influenced converted document content.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The earliest causal origin is eeddf1348f351c92355d010ced56c3b511ca8f46: the initial document-export implementation created node/ExportHandler.js with Math.floor(Math.random()*new Date().getTime()), a hard-coded /tmp/eplite_export_ path, fs.writeFile(), and converter output at a sibling predictable path. b13fbbfd73ab18f69d45de382ffb1fc51fe96f1f added the same design to import two days later. Commits 4fc4a3538148bc995fff989794e91779ed4c847f and b0976a292f70c2c6d344bafd2793aed09027f74b later changed the token formula to Math.random()*0xFFFFFFFF, reducing it to the advisory's exact 32-bit form, but they did not originate the insecure shared-temp predictable-name mechanism.

review_record.bug_semantics: The soffice-backed import/export paths placed working files in the shared directory returned by os.tmpdir() under names derived from non-cryptographic Math.random(), without exclusive creation or no-follow protection. A local user able to predict or race a token could pre-create a symlink at an export source path (or a converter destination path); ExportHandler's fs.writeFile then followed the link and truncated/wrote the linked target with exported HTML, subject to the Etherpad process's filesystem privileges. The import conversion destination was likewise predictable and could receive partially attacker-controlled converted upload content. Shared-host local access and a target writable by Etherpad are required.

review_record.reasoning: The vulnerability existed when the reachable export feature was first added in 2011: a non-CSPRNG token selected a shared-/tmp pathname and ordinary fs.writeFile followed an attacker-planted symlink. The later switch from Math.random()*time to the advisory's exact 32-bit Math.random()*0xFFFFFFFF expression did not create the security property; its parent was already vulnerable, so selecting the 2011 rewrite or later TypeScript moves would confuse textual provenance with causal origin. The immediate parent of eeddf1348f351c92355d010ced56c3b511ca8f46 lacks both the handler and its route, making eeddf1348f351c92355d010ced56c3b511ca8f46 the smallest real BIC; it is an ordinary one-parent commit, not a squash requiring decomposition. The import path joined the same vulnerable lifecycle in b13fbbfd73ab18f69d45de382ffb1fc51fe96f1f. Commit 8c6104c5d5daf41f0d454acc04d42dffa0e0d996 directly closes the advisory's predictability window in both handlers with 128-bit CSPRNG tokens and first ships in 3.1.0, after the last vulnerable 3.0.0 tag. Although the later fix commit has Claude co-author trailers and the advisory credits Claude, the protocol expressly limits attribution to the BIC commit object. The BIC is human-authored/committed and contains no AI marker, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated environment-key holder can supply a run-metadata operation whose unconstrained key is a JSONHero path such as $.__proto__.polluted. applyMetadataOperations passes that key to JSONHeroPath.set on a normal cloned object without rejecting __proto__, constructor, or prototype segments, so the write reaches Object.prototype in the shared webapp process; inherited attacker properties then corrupt unrelated Prisma and metrics objects across tenants and can crash the process.
audit_record.flaw_origin: PR #1563 added the metadata-operations API and, in its member commit cf80a02d23d99b0f4eebe4ac5eb42059f34b2b3d, created packages/core/src/v3/runMetadata/operations.ts with JSONHeroPath(operation.key).set(...) while simultaneously defining every keyed operation schema with key: z.string(). The endpoint's API-key-authenticated request body was therefore connected directly to a prototype-walking setter with no dangerous-segment validation from the feature's first implementation.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the raw BIC commit object names human author and committer Eric Allam <eallam@icloud.com>, contains only GitButler metadata headers and the subject 'Implement run metadata updates from ancestor tasks', and has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI-attribution trailer.

At cf80a02d23d99b0f4eebe4ac5eb42059f34b2b3d, apps/webapp/app/routes/api.v1.runs.$runId.metadata.ts:11-19 parses UpdateMetadataRequestBody and passes it with the authenticated environment to updateMetadataService; apiBuilder.server.ts:472-489 authenticates an API key. The same BIC adds schemas/common.ts:11-56 with key: z.string() for set/delete/append/remove/increment and creates operations.ts:20-26 with new JSONHeroPath(operation.key).set(newMetadata, operation.value); its service applies those operations to request-selected run metadata. git blame -L 20,26 cf80a02d... attributes every vulnerable line to cf80a02d..., and git log cf80a02d... -S'new JSONHeroPath(operation.key)' selects that commit.
