GitHub squash-landed the two-member PR as a69aada2799626d3afbfc1eb6550611ca2444a4d.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated network client can complete the RTMP handshake/connect/createStream/publish sequence and receive NetStream.Publish.Start because SRS treats RTMP publishing as permitted unless an operator explicitly enables a vhost security policy (or supplies a separate hook/token control). In the default state, SrsSecurity::check returns success immediately when security.enabled is false, so the publish path has no mandatory authentication boundary.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 33c586181de6b3a0cee61022066cb6e61c666972 first completed the FMLE publish command path in trunk/src/core/srs_core_rtmp.cpp: it consumed SrsPublishPacket and unconditionally emitted onFCPublish/onStatus NetStream.Publish.Start, with no credential or authorization decision. Its immediate parent only handled releaseStream/FCPublish/createStream and returned before consuming or accepting publish. Commit 75f2607685814b86ad030df703834cf06f91447f later added optional vhost allow/deny security with a false default and an explicit allow-all bypass, preserving rather than originating the already unauthenticated publish behavior.

BIC object: `git cat-file commit 33c586181de6b3a0cee61022066cb6e61c666972` records the single parent e598616e14e4875bc5c7fcaf3ad981e7c992753e, human author/committer winlin <winterserver@126.com>, timestamp 2013-10-22, and no trailers. The advisory reference https://github.com/ossrs/srs/releases/tag/v5.0-r3 points to v5.0.213 but that release preserves the bypass; the reporter likewise explicitly says 5.0.213 is vulnerable. Therefore neither v5.0-r3 nor any later commit through HEAD is a fix, and fix_sha/direct_fix_sha are justified nulls.

Current attack path: trunk/src/app/srs_app_rtmp_conn.cpp identifies the remote client and stream, calls security_->check, and then starts FMLE/Flash publishing. With the default-false configuration, trunk/src/app/srs_app_security.cpp returns success before evaluating any rules, allowing an unauthenticated client to reach start_fmle_publish and receive NetStream.Publish.Start unless a deployment adds an independent control.

A remote client on TCP/1935 can complete RTMP negotiation and a publish command without credentials; SRS returns NetStream.Publish.Start and accepts publisher traffic. Later functional media fanout permits content injection, stream-name occupation, and resource/bandwidth abuse. The referenced reporter PoC uses connect -> createStream -> publish and treats NetStream.Publish.Start as confirmation. The public report expressly says this is missing authentication/insecure default configuration, not memory corruption or code execution; therefore the NVD/GHSA arbitrary-code-execution wording is not supported by its cited technical report or by the audited source path.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The manage-downloads admin deletion handler accepted attacker-controlled POST fields `file` and `file_name` independently of the integer `file_id`; when `unlinkfile=1`, it concatenated the configured download directory with `file` and passed the result to `unlink()`. Neither the original `trim()` nor the later `sanitize_text_field()` removes `../` segments or proves containment, so an authenticated administrator holding the normal delete nonce could alter the hidden `file` field and delete an arbitrary server file outside the download directory. Deleting a critical file such as wp-config.php can cause denial of service and can enable follow-on site compromise/RCE.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable trust boundary was present in the first public upstream source revision, WordPress Plugin SVN r7446 (2007-01-21): `trunk/downloadmanager/download-manager.php` read `$_POST['file']` and used it in `unlink($file_path.'/'.$file)` rather than deriving the path from the database row selected by `file_id`. Later renames, SVN-to-Git deployment, sanitization, and formatting preserved that mechanism. Git commit d3470a8971d9043438c8aad281cf37d14fefa208 fixed the root cause by accepting only `file_id`, reloading the downloads-table row, and unlinking the stored `$file->file` value.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent — the canonical BIC is SVN changeset r7446, whose commit metadata is author `GamerZ`, timestamp `2007-01-21 10:26:57`, and exact log message `WP-DownloadManager First Commit`; SVN exposes no separate committer or trailer block, and the revision has no Co-Authored-By/Generated-with/bot marker.
evidence: Advisory: https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-w2w8-j4gc-v26q identifies CVE-2026-2426 as path traversal through the deletion `file` parameter, affecting all versions through 1.69 and fixed in 1.69.1; its first-party fix reference is https://github.com/lesterchan/wp-downloadmanager/commit/d3470a8971d9043438c8aad281cf37d14fefa208.

The same commit changes the plugin version from 1.69 to 1.69.1 and its message is `Fetch file using file_id again instead of relying/trusting form post file POST param`.

Deleting a critical file such as wp-config.php can cause availability/integrity loss and may enable code execution through reconfiguration. The nonce and capability check prevent an unauthenticated path but do not bind the posted pathname to the selected database row.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated WordPress administrator can submit a download_path such as WP_CONTENT_DIR . '/../..'. review_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated WordPress administrator with the plugin's manage_downloads capability can submit a download_path such as WP_CONTENT_DIR . '/../../etc'. Versions 1.68.11 through 1.69 compare only the uncanonicalized string prefix with WP_CONTENT_DIR, so the traversal-bearing value passes and is persisted. The Add/Edit File browser then recursively enumerates that resolved directory, an administrator can register a selected file, and the download handler concatenates the persisted base path with the selected relative name and serves it with readfile(), exposing files outside wp-content (subject to the configured per-file permission). Before 1.68.11 the setting was even less constrained and accepted arbitrary paths directly.
review_record.flaw_origin: a141c14127eb8d72413ac6a11dd3e7ad66aef9b1 is the smallest single-parent commit that first added the vulnerable WP_CONTENT_DIR prefix validator. Its substr($download_path, 0, strlen(WP_CONTENT_DIR)) comparison is lexical, not canonical filesystem containment, so '..' components retain the approved textual prefix while resolving outside it. The commit simultaneously identifies itself as release 1.68.11. Its immediate parent directly stores download_path and contains no prefix-validator lines; thus the specific prefix-check bypass is absent there, although the older unrestricted setting already allowed the same confidentiality impact without needing traversal.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An attacker can place OSC/CSI control bytes in a filesystem entry name. When a user scans that entry in `dua i`, marks it, and quits without deleting it, the marked `PathBuf` is taken from the TUI mark pane. After `drop(terminal)` has restored the real terminal, the program passed `path.display()` directly to `println!`. No encoding or control-character filtering occurred at that output boundary, so a terminal emulator interpreted the embedded bytes rather than displaying an inert path, enabling such effects as terminal-title spoofing or clipboard manipulation.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Single-parent commit 017cbd7b4c3e57e1a98fbc595159be39bc97c708 implemented the marked-path-on-exit feature end to end: it added `MarkPane::into_paths`, extracted the remaining marked filesystem paths from the application, and added `println!("{}", path.display())` after the terminal object was dropped. That commit first created both the attacker-controlled path flow and the unsanitized post-TUI terminal sink; its immediate parent contains neither the extraction helper nor this print loop.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the BIC commit object identifies both author and committer as `Sebastian Thiel <sebastian.thiel@icloud.com>` and its complete message is `Print marked items upon exit if these are left in the marked pane` followed only by `Fixes #87`; there is no bot identity, `Co-Authored-By`, `Generated-with`, model name, or other AI trailer/marker on the BIC.

The frozen GHSA-2m2p-wc26-4j7x/CVE-2026-73479 bundle describes the same OSC/CSI injection and references b6e7cafd305c150834eb887e1de99bcdd3fca85d as affected history, not as the repair. Direct parent-tree verification: `git grep -n -E 'into_paths|println!\("\{\}", path\.display\(\)\)' c8d5650... -- src/main.rs src/interactive/widgets/mark.rs` returns no match, while the identical command on 017cbd... returns `into_paths` at mark.rs:105, its call at main.rs:99, and the raw print at main.rs:117. The BIC source shows `drop(terminal)` and stdout flush before that print. Feature intent is independently recorded by https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/issues/87, which asked to print marked paths and whose maintainer stated that v2.13 would print them on quit. Version boundary: c8d5650be77e000801b282c4c0a3861e710de6d8 is exactly tag v2.12.2; `merge-base --is-ancestor` shows the BIC absent from v2.12.2 and present in v2.13.0. `git tag --contains 017cbd...` begins at v2.13.0 and includes every dua-cli tag through v2.41.1. The direct fix is absent from v2.41.1 and is an ancestor of v2.42.0; v2.42.0's signed tag/release notes explicitly list `sanitize control characters in marked path output`. Fix: https://github.com/Byron/dua-cli/pull/366 and a2d375d7fdb4eecc287ad87715a3f021951e3e6d replace direct display with control-character filtering. Review commit 8521d0d0231a6e95b7b9cc350b2eb2fc570a2833 narrows filtering to terminal stdout so redirected machine-readable paths stay raw. Landing merge f515d36174efeba2cdc2148fbb684f201df9ddad has parents b6e7cafd305c150834eb887e1de99bcdd3fca85d and 8521d0d0231a6e95b7b9cc350b2eb2fc570a2833; `git diff f515d...^1 f515d... -- src/main.rs` shows the final `marked_path_for_output` helper, `stdout.is_terminal()` gate, sanitized print, and regression test. `git grep` on the merge tree finds the helper and sanitized call at src/main.rs:64 and :194 and no raw `println!("{}", path.display())`. Ancestry checks prove 017cbd... -> a2d375... -> f515d.... BIC-only AI evidence: `git show -s --format='author=%an <%ae>%ncommitter=%cn <%ce>%n%B' 017cbd...` returns the same human author/committer and only the two-line subject/`Fixes #87` message quoted in `ai_marker`.

review_record.bug_semantics: A local attacker can create a filesystem entry whose name contains terminal control bytes such as ESC-led OSC or CSI sequences. When a victim runs the interactive TUI, marks that entry, and quits, dua-cli tears down the TUI/terminal guard and then prints each remaining marked PathBuf with println!("{}", path.display()) to stdout without encoding or filtering control characters. On an attached terminal those bytes are interpreted rather than displayed, permitting terminal-title spoofing, clipboard manipulation, and terminal-dependent integrity/confidentiality effects; ratatui's protected in-TUI rendering is bypassed because this output occurs after the TUI exits.

primary_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated backend user with backend.manage_editor could save attacker-controlled LESS in Editor Settings -> Markup Styles. audit_record.bug_semantics: A backend user with backend.manage_branding can persist attacker-controlled custom_css. BrandSetting::compileCss() concatenates that value into LESS input, and LESS escape syntax can preserve a literal </style><script> payload in the compiled output. The shared backend layout emits BrandSetting::renderCss() inside a style element, so an unsanitized cache miss or cache hit permits stored XSS for later backend-page viewers.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 1203043a457dee3c298d7dd54289a866234cbb74 is the smallest first-writer: it directly changed modules/backend/models/BrandSettings.php from parsing only bundled custom.less to parsing that file concatenated with self::get('custom_css'). Its immediate parent already had the settings/compiler framework but did not connect custom_css to the LESS parser. The commit is a one-parent direct source edit, not an aggregate, import, move, revert, or release carrier.

primary_record.bug_semantics: A backend user holding backend.manage_branding can store attacker-controlled LESS in Settings -> Customize Backend -> Styles. BrandSetting::compileCss() concatenates custom_css into the LESS input; LESS escape syntax such as ~"</style><script>alert(1)</script><style>" preserves HTML delimiter and script text in the compiled result. BrandSetting::renderCss() returned that result without HTML sanitization, and modules/backend/layouts/_custom_styles.php echoed it inside a <style> element on backend pages, so the stored </style> breakout executes script for backend viewers.
primary_record.flaw_origin: Commit 1203043a457dee3c298d7dd54289a866234cbb74 first changed BrandSettings.php from parsing only the bundled custom.less file to parsing that file concatenated with self::get('custom_css'), while the compiled output was persisted/rendered without stripping HTML tags. The immediate parent already had the custom_css settings field and the style sink, but did not feed custom_css into the compiler, so this one-line data-flow addition is the smallest real BIC rather than later cache, rename, refactor, or error-handling commits.

primary_record.bug_semantics: The CMS controller admitted a backend user possessing any one CMS Theme Editor permission, but its AJAX handlers trusted the request-controlled template type and did not re-check the permission mapped to that type. A pages-only user could therefore open, create, save, delete, commit, or reset partials, layouts, content, or assets by crafting the handler parameters. The constructor also registered every template widget, including AssetList, for every admitted CMS user; AssetList's upload path processed a file without first binding the request to the active theme, so a user without cms.manage_assets could reach an unauthorized upload into the active theme's assets.
primary_record.flaw_origin: Single-parent commit 71a5dd67ab9e0d0da7caabd3fb5aaa3d86bb45e5 introduced the exploitable design as new code: modules/cms/controllers/Index.php used the section-wide cms.* gate, instantiated every TemplateList and AssetList unconditionally, and dispatched request-supplied type values into load/create/save/delete operations without a type-specific authorization check. The same commit introduced AssetList.php with constructor-time checkUploadPostback() upload processing and no validateRequestTheme() call in that upload path, while expanding modules/cms/ServiceProvider.php to register distinct cms.manage_content/assets/pages/layouts permissions. Its parent had only a skeletal CMS ServiceProvider and had neither Index.php nor AssetList.php, so the permission boundary and bypass surface first coexist in this commit.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated backend user could submit the self-service account save handler with an attacker-chosen form_context such as update. FormController trusted that POST value over the server-selected myaccount context, so Users::formExtendFields treated the request as an administrative user form and admitted role, individual-permission, and superuser-related fields into the form widget's save data. The handler still selected the attacker's own User model, allowing protected authorization attributes to be mass-updated and the account to gain higher backend privileges.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 94a4ccb6abccd025e7e201590999061574ffdeb9 made the Users controller's self-service mysettings action unrestricted by setting requiredPermissions to null. That small authorization change was the first point at which ordinary authenticated backend users could reach the already-existing unsafe composition of mysettings_onSave and POST-controlled FormController context selection; its parent still required backend.manage_users for the controller, so the low-privilege attack path was absent there.

audit_record.bug_semantics: ScpClient.Download(string, DirectoryInfo) starts a recursive SCP receive and trusts the filename captured from each server-controlled C (file) or D (directory) protocol record. It joins that unvalidated value to the current local download directory and then creates the directory or opens the file for writing. A malicious, compromised, or MITM server can therefore supply ../ components (and, after the later Path.Combine form, rooted paths) to escape the caller's destination and create or overwrite any path writable by the client process. Exploitation requires the victim to initiate a recursive directory download from the attacker-controlled endpoint.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit d96c93abb2f9409281bfb12d2da8622470a4b3e3 first added ScpClient and its recursive directory-download implementation. In Renci.SshClient/Renci.SshNet/ScpClient.NET.cs it parsed arbitrary remote C/D record names and used them directly in local directory creation and FileInfo construction without requiring a single safe path component. Commit 266dbaefe6c1f2bff2ea00c9ac14a246d37079d9 later changed the string concatenations to Path.Combine but did not introduce the trust-boundary flaw; renames, line-ending changes, and the 2023 partial-class merge likewise only carried the existing mechanism forward.

review_record.bug_semantics: Before 0.14.0, c3p0 shipped serializable/indirectly serializable JDBC DataSource and ConnectionPoolDataSource beans with public no-argument getConnection() and getPooledConnection() methods but no explicit BeanInfo excluding those method names. java.beans.Introspector therefore exposed connection and pooledConnection as readable bean properties. Exploitation additionally requires the relevant c3p0 datasource, a susceptible JDBC driver, and an automatic bean-property-reading carrier on the classpath.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Before 0.12.0, c3p0 exposed userOverridesAsString as a writable JavaBean/JNDI Reference property containing HexAsciiSerializedMap[<hex Java serialization stream>]. WrapperConnectionPoolDataSource parsed property resets and initial values with C3P0ImplUtils.parseUserOverridesAsString(), which hex-decoded attacker-controlled bytes and passed them to SerializableUtils.fromByteArray() without an allowlist. A crafted serialized ConnectionPoolDataSource or javax.naming.Reference could therefore trigger gadget deserialization and code execution; the historical mchange-commons-java Reference behavior amplified this with remote factoryClassLocation loading.

primary_record.bug_semantics: Before 0.12.0, c3p0 represented the writable JavaBean property userOverridesAsString as 'HexAsciiSerializedMap[' plus hex-encoded Java serialization bytes. C3P0ImplUtils.parseUserOverridesAsString() stripped that wrapper, hex-decoded attacker-controlled bytes, and passed them to SerializableUtils.fromByteArray() without an allowlist. WrapperConnectionPoolDataSource invoked this parser from its vetoable-change listener whenever the property was reset, and ComboPooledDataSource exported the property through its javax.naming.Reference. An attacker able to supply a crafted property value directly, through a serialized ConnectionPoolDataSource, or through a JNDI Reference could therefore trigger gadget deserialization. In combination with the dependency's then-ungated indirect JNDI Reference/factoryClassLocation handling, this could download and execute attacker code; independently, deserializing arbitrary objects from a writable bean string was unsafe.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An attacker-controlled Typebot imported from JSON could retain a Script block whose content the preview API returned as a client-side action. @typebot.io/js then compiled that untrusted content with Function/AsyncFunction directly in the authenticated builder page. Code run there could make same-origin fetch requests with the victim's session, enumerate the victim's user/workspace credentials, receive decrypted credential data from credentials.getCredentials, and exfiltrate API keys, OAuth tokens, and passwords. The workspace form of getCredentials also authorized the supplied workspace but, at the vulnerable snapshot, did not bind the requested credential ID to that workspace.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The single member commit behind PR #194 introduced all three causal pieces together: file import accepted JSON.parse(fileContent) without marking executable blocks untrusted, the viewer converted Script/Code block content into a codeToExecute client action, and the new @typebot.io/js executeCode implementation invoked Function on that content in the page context. It supplied neither a trust boundary for imported bots nor a sandbox/credentialless execution context.

primary_record.reasoning: The vulnerability is not merely that Typebot intentionally supports scripts; it is a missing trust transition. PR #194 made imported JSON executable in the authenticated preview origin by carrying block content through codeToExecute to a raw Function call. That gives an imported attacker's code the victim's builder origin and session, from which the credential-list/get endpoints provide the confidentiality impact described by the GHSA. Line history proves later AsyncFunction conversion, renames, and refactors preserved the same unsandboxed mechanism. PR #194 was squash-merged, so treating landed 1a3869ae6d9fa92fc71ef9d981bfffb8e4ee4ecc as irreducible would be wrong; the public PR exposes one original member, 3487850b9f4808617d347ddde4d9701f56662894, whose tree and parent exactly equal the landed squash tree and parent. That member is therefore the smallest reconstructable BIC. Its immediate parent has no packages/js executor path, while the BIC creates the importer, server dispatch, and Function sink together. The identical landed tree is present before the first @typebot.io/js release and remains in 0.9.14. Fix a68f0c91790af8f52f17557f4aa202e966e7e579 directly establishes an imported-code trust flag and a credentialless worker for preview, and it is the sole relevant boundary commit between js-v0.9.14 and js-v0.9.15. review_record.bug_semantics: An attacker-controlled imported Typebot could contain a Script block whose code was returned as a client-side action and compiled and executed by @typebot.io/js in the preview page with AsyncFunction/Function. Preview ran under the victim's authenticated app.typebot.io browser context, so the script could issue same-origin credentialed requests. It could enumerate the victim's credentials and call credentials.getCredentials to obtain decrypted OpenAI keys, Google tokens, SMTP secrets, and other stored credential data, then exfiltrate them. The user-scoped getCredentials branch did bind the record to user.id; the workspace branch checked that the victim could write the supplied workspace but fetched the credential by id without additionally binding it to that workspace. Either way, arbitrary script in the victim's session defeated the intended principal boundary. The missing control was distrust/sandboxing of imported client-executed code during privileged preview, not JavaScript syntax validation.
review_record.flaw_origin: The affected @typebot.io/js executor lineage was created by pull-request member commit 3487850b9f4808617d347ddde4d9701f56662894. It added packages/js/src/features/blocks/logic/code/utils/executeCode.ts with Function(...args, content) and invoked it for server-supplied code actions, with no import provenance, preview trust decision, consent, or sandbox. GitHub squash commit 1a3869ae6d9fa92fc71ef9d981bfffb8e4ee4ecc has the same parent and tree, so it is only the landed aggregate object, not the smallest recoverable commit object. Later commits renamed Code to Script, added async support, moved the package/path, and exposed an Execute on client toggle defaulting true; those preserved or expanded the already-present sink rather than introducing it. A still earlier legacy bot-engine Code-step executor existed in e3e07ddd4dbae6e7b893a0d6be9f12b80d1a6c9c, but it is not the affected @typebot.io/js file/package lineage: 3487850b created the distinct V2 embed package implementation that was subsequently released as @typebot.io/js.

audit_record.bug_semantics: PyBlade passed attacker-controlled template expressions to Python eval with a live rendering context. In the 0.1.x renderer, directive conditions and iterables reached eval(expression, {}, context), which restores normal builtins and also permits Python object-graph traversal. The 0.2.0-alpha rewrite retained reachable raw-eval and unrestricted attribute/method paths. The advisory's narrower _is_safe_ast Constant-rooted bypass is not the reachable 0.1.8-alpha mechanism: that validator rejects a Constant-rooted Attribute and the tagged renderer has no sandbox.safe_eval caller. Commit 62c95c472fbd9ca5630a989ddec9d8899256726a replaces the active expression evaluator with a restricted AST interpreter that rejects underscore-prefixed attributes.

primary_record.bug_semantics: Attacker-controlled template expressions were evaluated as Python with a live rendering context. In the 0.1.x interpolation path, `{{ x.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}` passed a context-rooted dotted expression to raw `eval`; an empty globals dictionary is not a sandbox, because Python attribute traversal from any ordinary context object reaches the process object graph and can recover classes, module globals, and command-execution primitives. The 0.2.0-alpha rewrite retained the defect: `ExpressionEvaluator` either walked arbitrary attributes/methods or routed expressions containing an operator to `safe_eval`, which called raw `eval` with only `__builtins__` emptied. Commit 62c95c472fbd9ca5630a989ddec9d8899256726a replaced those paths with an AST interpreter that rejects underscore-prefixed attributes and restricts callable methods/builtins.
primary_record.flaw_origin: The smallest real BIC for the reported `{{ ... }}` SSTI path is 2afc2aa5c29a413db5bf26fb0ef39fc6a18fec78 (`Add the possibility to call variables methods in the template`). It widened both interpolation regexes from simple `\w+` names to arbitrary expressions and added `variable_value = eval(".".join(expression), {}, context)` in `pyblade/engine/parser.py`. Its immediate parent only looked up a simple captured name and could not send dotted interpolation syntax to Python evaluation. The later c539c2a5c3bfb0e07d41b35a0e4b1cf3fb51b89a split/moved this same sink to `pyblade/engine/parsing/variables.py`, and 806f68cdab59694b780f3af0f0a6f7a535bbd08d replaced it with another unsafe evaluator for 0.2.0-alpha; neither later commit is the origin. The issue's separate assertion that `_is_safe_ast` in 0.1.8-alpha accepts a Constant-rooted `''.__class__` payload is contradicted by that tag's tree and by execution: the Attribute branch returns false unless the base is an allowed Name/attribute pair, and the sandbox is not called by the tagged rendering path. review_record.bug_semantics: PyBlade evaluates expressions embedded in templates as Python. In the v0.1.4-alpha tag (and still in v0.1.8-alpha/v.0.1.9-alpha), PyBlade.render calls Parser.parse, whose directive handlers pass template-controlled @if/@for and other expressions to eval(..., {}, context); because the globals mapping omits __builtins__, Python inserts the normal builtins, so a template can call __import__ and execute commands. The v0.2.0-alpha rewrite keeps the vulnerability through Processor.render_variable -> ExpressionEvaluator.evaluate -> safe_eval -> eval(expression, {"__builtins__": SAFE_BUILTINS}, context); expressions containing parentheses take that direct-eval path, and Python object-model chains can recover dangerous classes/globals. The advisory's narrower claimed v0.1.8/v.0.1.9 _is_safe_ast Constant bypass is contradicted by the tagged source: for every ast.Attribute whose value is not ast.Name, including ''.__class__, the function reaches its unconditional return False, and no released engine code imports or calls sandbox.safe_eval. Thus the releases are vulnerable, but through reachable raw eval rather than the alleged AST-validation bypass, and the tracked vulnerable tag boundary is at least as early as v0.1.4-alpha.

audit_record.bug_semantics: getFilenameFromUrl accepts a decoded request pathname when it merely starts with the configured publicPath pathname, rejects dot-dot only when UP_PATH_REGEXP sees `..` as a complete path segment, and then slices the accepted string at publicPathPathname.length before joining the suffix to outputPath. With a non-slash-terminated publicPath `/assets`, `/assets../.env` passes the prefix check and guard because `..` remains embedded in the `assets..` segment, but the fixed-offset slice yields `../.env`, so path.join resolves one directory above outputPath. Disclosure requires a physical or custom output filesystem, such as writeToDisk; the default memfs and default publicPath `auto`/`/` do not expose this path, and URL normalization limits this bypass to one parent directory.

review_record.bug_semantics: getFilenameFromUrl treats a textual publicPath prefix as containment. With a non-slash-terminated publicPath such as /assets, /assets../.env passes pathname.startsWith('/assets'). The 2024 UP_PATH_REGEXP guard tests path.normalize('./' + pathname), where the only '..' is embedded in the segment 'assets..' and therefore is not rejected. Slicing at publicPathPathname.length then changes the same characters into the standalone relative path '../.env'; path.join(outputPath, '../.env') escapes one directory above outputPath. The escaped file is disclosed when the selected outputFileSystem exposes physical files (not the default isolated memfs), notably writeToDisk === true or a supplied filesystem. URL parsing/normalization limits this particular bypass to one parent level; publicPath 'auto' maps to '/' and is not affected.

primary_record.bug_semantics: An EventStream subscriber was authorized only at dashboard-subscription granularity, then placed in a global client registry. The finished-event LogEntry included the command's accumulated Output, while OutputChunk exposed live bytes, so a low-privileged authenticated dashboard user could observe metadata and output for an action whose logs that user was not authorized to view.

audit_record.bug_semantics: With saveLogs enabled, a caller authorized to execute an action can supply a nonempty, nonduplicate StartAction UniqueTrackingId containing slash and .. segments. OliveTin accepts that string, stores it as the log entry's ExecutionTrackingID, interpolates it into the .yaml and .log filenames, and passes those names to path.Join. path.Join cleans the traversal segments, so ioutil.WriteFile writes both files outside the configured log directories to attacker-selected paths writable by the OliveTin process.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The existing API-to-executor path already accepted arbitrary client tracking strings. PR #300's sole member commit fe991045b5bd9c7fbe57bb83a12a56deca68ef06 first made that unsafe value filesystem-relevant by adding stepSaveLog, composing filenames from ExecutionTrackingID without validation or basename confinement, joining them to configured directories, and writing them. audit_record.bug_semantics: A caller-supplied value for an action argument whose type is configured as regex:<pattern> is accepted when Go regexp.MatchString reports a match, then substituted verbatim into the action's Shell command and executed through sh -c. A regex can therefore admit shell syntax such as POSIX command substitution; even after OliveTin added a Shell-mode unsafe-type guard, that guard compared only a fixed set of exact type names and did not recognize the regex: prefix, so the value still reached the shell unescaped.

The new prefix branch made that previously impossible configuration executable without adding a shell-safety constraint, creating the command-injection path. GitHub squash-landed the member as c97fd60c2508ddf99ebc7c03570683811c476de9 with the same tree and parent. Later commit c917d1b1e7a2a90acec79760cb1ff18ffae82409 added checkShellArgumentSafety but omitted regex: types, preserving rather than originating the flaw.

review_record.bug_semantics: A Shell-mode action may declare an argument type beginning with regex:. The custom pattern is checked with regexp.MatchString, but checkShellArgumentSafety historically compared only exact names in a fixed unsafe-type map and therefore allowed every regex:-prefixed type. The accepted attacker value is inserted without shell quoting into the configured command and executed through sh -c. Thus a value such as $(touch /tmp/rce_proof) passes a superficially restrictive regex that excludes ;|&<> when the pattern permits $, parentheses, and the command text, then executes by POSIX command substitution. Partial-match regex behavior could widen the bypass further, but is not required for the advisory's command-substitution attack.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /images handler accepts request.query.src and passes it to imageProcessor. For any value beginning with http:// or https://, imageProcessor treats it as external, skips all local-path validation, and calls fetch(src) without a destination allowlist or network-address restriction. An attacker can therefore make the EverShop server request attacker-selected external or internal HTTP(S) resources, including link-local metadata services, producing blind SSRF.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 created both the front-store images handler and imageProcessor.ts. Its newly written external-URL branch classified a URL only by its http/https prefix and then directly executed fetch(src); the validation in the same function applied only to non-external filesystem paths. This is the first repository commit that contains both the public request path and the flawed server-side fetch mechanism, not a later move, refactor, revert, or release aggregate.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /images endpoint accepts an image source and sends the resulting bytes to Sharp. For SVG input, imageProcessor deliberately rasterizes at density 300 with limitInputPixels disabled and performs no structural bound on use-element shadow-tree depth or pattern-tile dimensions. A crafted SVG can therefore make the underlying SVG renderer consume unbounded CPU or memory until the application server, and potentially the host, is denied service.

review_record.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /images endpoint accepted an attacker-selected http(s) src, fetched the response into a Buffer, detected SVG through sharp, and rasterized it at density 300 with limitInputPixels explicitly disabled before encoding with toBuffer(). A crafted SVG containing deeply nested use-element shadow trees or enormous pattern tiles therefore drives unbounded CPU/memory consumption in sharp/libvips and can deny service. The public attack described by the advisory chains the unrestricted external fetch with this unsafe SVG rasterization.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The public GraphQL Query.order resolver accepts an attacker-controlled order UUID and loads the matching order without authenticating the caller or constraining the query to the caller's customer/session identity. An unauthenticated caller who obtains a valid UUID can therefore traverse the returned Order fields and nested resolvers to read customer email/name, billing and shipping addresses, purchased items, totals, payment state, and shipment data belonging to another customer.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e changed the order lookup from an integer order_id plus tokenPayload-derived customer_id/sid ownership predicates to a string UUID lookup alone: it deleted extraction of customerId and sid and deleted both ownership/session constraints, leaving query.where('uuid', '=', id). audit_record.bug_semantics: An attacker-controlled account value can be reflected by the REST error path in ExceptionMessage and the JSON response body. The account_rse_usage WebUI error callbacks passed the raw jqXHR.responseText through string concatenation to jQuery.html(), so the victim's browser parsed payload markup such as an img onerror handler in the Rucio WebUI origin instead of displaying it as text. A crafted link therefore executes script when an authenticated user opens it, exposing the WebUI token/session and permitting actions with the victim's authority.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 045193619da3087de74d77ec0f715ce57c1ed035 created lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account_rse_usage.js and, in both nested request error callbacks, wrote $("#results").html('<font color="red">' + jqXHR['responseText'] + '</font>'). That new page combined an attacker-influenced server response with an HTML parsing sink without encoding it; this is the concrete sink exercised by the advisory's account_rse_usage?account= payload.

audit_record.bug_semantics: picklescan disassembles pickle GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL references and, in the default scan result, counts a finding only when the referenced module/name matches its hard-coded unsafe-globals blocklist. Through v0.0.34 the blocklist omitted both the serialized global _io.FileIO and urllib.request.urlopen, so a crafted pickle could open an arbitrary local file and pass that file object as the body of an attacker-directed HTTP request without either global being counted as dangerous. A consumer relying on the scan could then deserialize the payload, causing arbitrary file read plus SSRF/data exfiltration.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The initial scanner implementation introduced the incomplete-denylist security model: src/picklescan/scanner.py enumerated selected suspicious globals and scan_pickle_bytes incremented issues_count only for exact blocklist matches, silently leaving unlisted callable globals such as _io.FileIO and urllib.request.urlopen outside the failing result. Later classification of unknown globals as Suspicious did not cure the default-pass behavior because only Dangerous globals incremented issues_count; the vulnerable mechanism therefore originates in the initial scanner commit rather than in a later refactor or blocklist expansion.

PR https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/pull/55 and release https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan/releases/tag/v0.0.35 identify the remediation. In the validated clone, `git log -L 14,24:src/picklescan/scanner.py c1d5abd...` attributes the original suspicious-globals dictionary to c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e, and `git log -L 77,89:src/picklescan/scanner.py c1d5abd...` shows that same new-file commit introduced scan_pickle_bytes with exact blocklist lookup and issues_count increment only on a match. `git cat-file -e 6a76b8c3ac67dc04181e600614ecf2a423cca326:src/picklescan/scanner.py` fails because the path is absent, while `git ls-tree -r --name-only` for that parent shows no src tree, directly verifying parent absence. At v0.0.34, src/picklescan/scanner.py:356-391 maps non-blocklisted globals to Suspicious but increments issues_count only for Dangerous entries, and its unsafe table at lines 110-186 contains neither _io.FileIO nor urllib.request. `git log -S` for both `"_io": {"FileIO"}` and `"urllib.request": "*"` finds only a01c58d5dd7960db557b849817c0ab83ab111ef1. audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerability is a scanner-detection bypass, not execution performed by picklescan itself: the scanner exposes pickle globals, but its default failing result is driven by a finite dangerous-global dictionary. The advisory's payload serializes io.FileIO as _io.FileIO to open a local file and then invokes urllib.request.urlopen with that file as an iterable request body, so omitting both globals permits the malicious pickle to avoid a Dangerous finding and creates the unsafe trust decision before downstream unpickling. History tracing distinguishes the true origin from later churn: f98f9bd89b16ab1b1b1b6366acddd1b2a4d36fe9 merely renamed _suspicious_globals to _unsafe_globals during PyTorch work, whereas c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e created both the finite blocklist and exact-match reporting logic in one direct, single-parent implementation commit. Its immediate parent has no scanner source at all, so the vulnerable mechanism is directly absent there; no squash/member decomposition or move is needed. The BIC shipped in the initial 0.0.1 code and is ancestral to v0.0.34, while the direct fix a01c58d5dd7960db557b849817c0ab83ab111ef1 is exactly tag v0.0.35 and adds the two missing dangerous globals. AI attribution is restricted to the BIC commit object: it has human author and committer identities, a plain one-line message, and no AI/co-author/generated trailers. Therefore the proven smallest BIC is human-authored and the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

primary_record.bug_semantics: OpenAM 16.0.6 installs the iPlanetDirectoryPro SSO cookie with com.sun.identity.cookie.httponly=false and com.iplanet.am.cookie.secure=false and without a SameSite default. audit_record.bug_semantics: The authenticated chat-user endpoint accepts q after only trimming it and requiring two characters, then Chat::searchUsers() applies the database driver's ordinary SQL-string escape and interpolates the result into LOWER(ud.display_name) LIKE '%%%s%%'. SQL-string escaping prevents a quote breakout but leaves the LIKE pattern metacharacters % and _ active. Thus q=%% or q=__ passes the length gate and broadens the predicate instead of searching for those literal characters, letting any logged-in user retrieve active users' IDs and display names and systematically enumerate accounts.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit a7275859a5d6bc19c20827fe1ec6f6d925ea6f27 introduced the chat feature, the authenticated user-search controller, and Chat::searchUsers() together. Its first implementation put attacker-controlled search text, protected only by the generic database escape(), inside a LIKE pattern and supplied neither wildcard escaping nor an SQL ESCAPE clause. Commit 1dd0432a900d85f712b26c6be07dd5f70511d868 later made the comparison case-insensitive and removed the is_visible restriction, but retained the already-flawed escape-plus-LIKE design; it expanded/rewrote the vulnerable search rather than originating the wildcard-injection mechanism.

review_record.bug_semantics: Any authenticated user can send GET /api/chat/users?q=%% (URL-encoded as %25%25) or q=__ and bypass the intended display-name substring filter. audit_record.bug_semantics: Stored XSS in the authenticated WebUI RSE-management flow. A privileged attacker can persist attacker-controlled markup in city, country_name, or ISP through the RSE creation path. The RSE list passes those stored values to DataTables as renderable data, while the RSE detail page concatenates them into HTML passed to jQuery.append. Viewing either page therefore parses the stored value as markup and can execute script in the victim's WebUI origin.

This is the original vulnerable implementation, not a merge, move, import, revert, or aggregate carrier.

primary_record.bug_semantics: An administrator-controlled RSE creation request can persist HTML/JavaScript in the city, country_name, or ISP metadata fields. The WebUI then treats those stored strings as markup in two victim-facing paths: lib/rucio/web/ui/static/rses.js passes the raw API objects directly to DataTables columns, and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/rse.js concatenates metadata values into HTML passed to jQuery.append. Loading the RSE Management list or an RSE detail page therefore executes the stored payload in the viewer's WebUI origin, where it can read JavaScript-accessible session/token material and act with the victim's authority.
primary_record.flaw_origin: Commit 8f1a24a568331b10f9d8fb099ef233af340b7735 introduced the RSE-management WebUI feature as one ordinary commit. The persistence API predated or existed independently of the browser view, but this commit first created the executable rendering sinks and the documented WebUI create/trigger lifecycle.

review_record.bug_semantics: Stored XSS in the authenticated WebUI RSE-management flow. A privileged attacker can create an RSE with HTML/JavaScript in city, country_name, or ISP; add_rse.js serializes those values unchanged into POST /rses/<RSE>, and the backend persists them. The advisory notes JavaScript-readable session/API tokens and same-origin privileged requests as impact amplifiers.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An attacker who can add an account identity can POST an identity string containing HTML or JavaScript to /accounts/<account>/identities. The backend stores that identity string and the account-identities GET endpoint returns it. On the WebUI account page, load_identities handed the returned objects directly to jQuery DataTables as data and selected the identity and type properties as columns. DataTables treated those string values as cell HTML, so merely viewing the affected account page inserted the persisted identity into the DOM and executed attacker-controlled script in the viewer's WebUI origin.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 4f67434304e5bd445c01a636d88113b76a68ef78 created the account-administration page and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account.js. Its new load_identities function passed the server response directly to DataTable with `data: data` and `columns: [{'data': 'identity'}, {'data': 'type'}]`, without encoding the identity before the HTML sink. The same feature commit also added the UI's identity-creation helper, completing the store-and-render path. The pre-existing backend identity model/API stored and returned the supplied identity as data; the vulnerability began when this commit added the unsafe browser rendering, not when later code was moved or refactored.

primary_record.bug_semantics: An attacker who can add an account identity can POST an identity string containing HTML or JavaScript to /accounts/<account>/identities. The backend stores that identity string and the account-identities GET endpoint returns it. On the WebUI account page, load_identities handed the returned objects directly to jQuery DataTables as data and selected the identity and type properties as columns. DataTables treated those string values as cell HTML, so merely viewing the affected account page inserted the persisted identity into the DOM and executed attacker-controlled script in the viewer's WebUI origin.
primary_record.flaw_origin: Commit 4f67434304e5bd445c01a636d88113b76a68ef78 created the account-administration page and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account.js. The same feature commit also added the UI's identity-creation helper, completing the store-and-render path. The pre-existing backend identity model/API stored and returned the supplied identity as data; the vulnerability began when this commit added the unsafe browser rendering, not when later code was moved or refactored.

review_record.bug_semantics: Stored XSS in the legacy Rucio WebUI account-identity table. A privileged attacker can use Admin > Account Management > an account > Add Account Identity (POST /proxy/accounts/<account>/identities) to persist an identity such as <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>. When a victim opens /ui/account?account=<account>, load_identities() obtains the stored identity through r.list_identities() and used to pass the returned objects directly to jQuery DataTables as `data: data`; the `identity` and `type` columns were therefore rendered as HTML rather than output-encoded text. JavaScript executes in the WebUI origin with the viewing user's authority, permitting token/cookie theft or authenticated actions. The closing change constructs a separate display object and HTML-encodes identity/type with `$('<div>').text(String(value)).html()` while retaining raw `$identity`/`$type` only for API operations.
review_record.flaw_origin: Commit 4f67434304e5bd445c01a636d88113b76a68ef78 (`[RUCIO-2849] RucioUI account admin pages`) is the smallest public first-writer. It created lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account.js and the account page, adding both the identity creation flow and load_identities(), whose DataTable consumed the server-returned identity objects without encoding. It is a normal one-parent feature commit, not a move, revert, release/backport, merge wrapper, or reconstructable squash; its parent had the identity-list API client but no account page, identities table, or vulnerable display sink.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and GemFire vector-store converters serialize a caller-supplied Filter.Key into a Lucene-style query string. Their escaping left tab, LF, CR, and U+3000 ideographic space unescaped, so a key can introduce token boundaries and operators such as OR; the resulting string is passed to the backend query parser, allowing an attacker to replace the intended metadata predicate with arbitrary query clauses.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 9334d7d540f8d0ee7cb09e44b272c95c2c159627 first added an affected backend and the causal pattern: ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.doKey() appended the metadata-prefixed Filter.Key directly to the query string with only trim(), while ElasticsearchVectorStore supplied that converted string to Elasticsearch queryString(). OpenSearch later copied the affected converter in 46e47849cec4b8a6fffbd13997f3cce4f886347b, and GemFire added the same kind of filter-query path in 833a856f51090f0eb98332db2341ce7a107af1fd. Later shared-converter refactors and partial escaping changed the location and reduced the character set but did not create the vulnerability or close the whitespace bypass.

audit_record.evidence: First-party advisory https://spring.io/security/cve-2026-47835 states that special characters could force arbitrary queries in Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and GemFire VectorDB and identifies affected Spring AI 1.0.0-1.0.8 and 1.1.0-1.1.7, fixed in 1.0.9 and 1.1.8; GHSA references direct commits https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/commit/2b20cfc8f478444f942d4be7a867d254441ff991 and https://github.com/spring-projects/spring-ai/commit/9787991aa1ed92c511131ddf4e142bd94051e6e7. In the validated full-history clone, git log -L 86,95:vector-stores/spring-ai-elasticsearch-store/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/vectorstore/ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.java 9334d7d... resolves the raw doKey implementation to the new-file commit 9334d7d540f8d0ee7cb09e44b272c95c2c159627; git log -S 'context.append(prefixedIdentifier.trim()).append(":");' confirms 9334d7d... added that statement and later fc1f92d11cacc79bdf8d41eb7f941a64fdf67482 only moved/refactored it. The BIC also added vector-stores/spring-ai-elasticsearch-store/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/vectorstore/ElasticsearchVectorStore.java, whose getElasticsearchSimilarityQuery() sends getElasticsearchQueryString(filterExpression) into queryString(...). Direct parent-tree check `git cat-file -e 8e50802eb8dd9044c15d7e75ad94ae618dca5c12:vector-stores/spring-ai-elasticsearch-store/src/main/java/org/springframework/ai/vectorstore/ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.java` fails because the path is absent, while the BIC adds it from /dev/null. GitHub's commit-to-pulls API returns [] for 9334d7d..., and the one-parent commit object contains the actual feature diff, so there is no squash member history to substitute. `git merge-base --is-ancestor` succeeds from 9334d7d... to v1.0.0 (fcd2803f36f35939c20ed152c9c1b0863fa35dcf), v1.1.0 (fa4c61eabeba0a69147b3c00a3b50380c1f25a75), and both fixes. At v1.0.8, AbstractFilterExpressionConverter.emitLuceneString() escapes ordinary space and Lucene punctuation but not tab/LF/CR/U+3000, and Elasticsearch doKey() routes the metadata field path through that helper. Direct fix 2b20cfc8f478444f942d4be7a867d254441ff991 adds cases for '\t', '\n', '\r', and '\u3000' plus regression tests for all three stores; its equivalent 1.0.x backport is 9787991aa1ed92c511131ddf4e142bd94051e6e7. `git tag --contains` maps 2b20cfc... to v1.1.8 and 9787991... to v1.0.9; ancestry checks place neither fix in v1.1.7/v1.0.8 respectively, and place each in its patched tag.
audit_record.reasoning: The security boundary is the construction of a backend query string, not merely the later helper method. The smallest affected-history commit that first made attacker-controlled metadata keys reach such a sink is 9334d7d..., which simultaneously introduced the Elasticsearch converter's unescaped doKey() and the queryString sink. The earlier similar Azure converter is not the BIC for this advisory because it enforces an allowedIdentifierNames whitelist and is not one of the affected products; 9334d7d... removed that safety in the newly affected backend. OpenSearch and GemFire are later ports of the same causal design. Refactors in 2026 centralized escaping and a partial hardening added ordinary-space handling, but the vulnerable capability already existed and the last vulnerable tags still failed to escape alternate whitespace. Both supported release lines then received the same four-character escaping patch at the documented fixed boundaries. The immediate parent lacks the affected converter and sink, the BIC predates both affected version lines, and the BIC commit object has no AI attribution signal; therefore the BIC-only verdict is NOT_AI.

review_record.bug_semantics: The default metadata-filter converters for Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and GemFire interpolate a Filter.Key into a Lucene/query_string expression. An embedded tab, newline, carriage return, or ideographic space (U+3000) was not backslash-escaped, so attacker-controlled key text could terminate or split the intended field token and inject Boolean/query syntax. The generated string is passed to Elasticsearch/OpenSearch queryString queries (including OpenSearch delete-by-query) or to GemFire as filterQuery, permitting execution of an arbitrary query rather than the intended metadata predicate.
review_record.flaw_origin: The earliest affected implementation is Elasticsearch support commit 9334d7d540f8d0ee7cb09e44b272c95c2c159627, which created ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.doKey and appended the trimmed metadata-prefixed key directly to the query string without syntax escaping. OpenSearch later copied the same unsafe doKey shape in 46e47849cec4b8a6fffbd13997f3cce4f886347b, and GemFire filter support introduced it in 78c5e001d39e40f0da1f5b7b2b78a38f2047c01f. March 2026 hardening routed these keys through emitLuceneString, but that helper still escaped only ordinary ASCII space and Lucene punctuation, leaving tab, LF, CR, and U+3000 exploitable until the advisory fixes.

audit_record.bug_semantics: A project-scoped owner member or lessee administrator who may PATCH a volume target but is not permitted by baremetal:volume:view_target_properties can change an unrelated allowed field and receive the complete updated target in the HTTP 200 response. PATCH authorizes baremetal:volume:update, loads and updates the existing target, and serializes new_target without applying the target-properties redaction used by GET/list, thereby disclosing pre-existing iSCSI connection data or credentials. POST had the same unredacted response shape, but its caller supplied the returned values; the advisory's confidentiality escalation is the PATCH disclosure of existing secrets.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The original volume-target REST API commit c380e05dbf84079b01fb3b0ea099ef9b293b9b3d created an admin-only PATCH response that returned the complete target, so it is the latent response-shape origin, not the security BIC. Commit 000bc72cc29b8637df496f2e6768281606a27058 later rewrote the representation to plain JSON without changing that behavior. The vulnerability first became real in e870bd34d0ccacbaef7f4e4def2535eb28f822b9: that commit expanded baremetal:volume:update from system-only access to system/project owner-member and lessee-admin access, introduced a stricter baremetal:volume:view_target_properties boundary, enforced the new boundary on GET/list, and left PATCH returning the full target without the new check. This is the smallest causal commit inside the advisory's affected version boundary.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The authenticated /v1/completions endpoint accepted an attacker-chosen outer list of text prompts or token-id prompt lists. The serving path preserved that outer cardinality, created one engine generator and request ID per element, merged all generators, and allocated streaming or non-streaming response state proportional to the number of prompts. audit_record.bug_semantics: PickleScan classified a pickle only from GLOBAL/INST/STACK_GLOBAL module-and-name references found in its opcode stream. A malicious pickle could import the unblocked pkgutil.resolve_name, call it by REDUCE with data such as 'os:system' to obtain a blocked callable without importing that callable, then invoke the returned callable with a second REDUCE. Because REDUCE arguments and returned stack values were not resolved into new globals, the scanner saw only pkgutil.resolve_name and reported no dangerous global while unpickling executed arbitrary code.

review_record.bug_semantics: In releases before 1.0.4, PickleScan extracted explicit GLOBAL, INST, and STACK_GLOBAL references and checked those names against a finite unsafe-global blocklist, but it did not interpret the callable/value flow produced by REDUCE. An attacker can therefore encode pkgutil.resolve_name as the only visible global, call it with a data string such as 'os:system' in a first REDUCE to obtain a blocked callable, and invoke that returned callable in a second REDUCE. Because pkgutil.resolve_name was not in the blocklist and the eventual os.system reference never appears as a pickle global, the malicious pickle had issues_count == 0 despite executing arbitrary code when unpickled. The gadget makes every blocklisted target reachable through the same indirection.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Legacy PyTorch serialization unpickles the first pickle to obtain MAGIC_NUMBER, so that value may be computed by a REDUCE callable rather than encoded as an INT/LONG opcode. picklescan's get_magic_number instead disassembled the first pickle and returned only the first opcode whose name contained INT or LONG. An attacker could encode eval('0x1950A86A20F9469CFC6C') as the first pickle: PyTorch obtains the correct magic number, while picklescan obtains None and rejects/abandons the PyTorch scan before examining the later pickle containing the dangerous payload. The file therefore remains loadable by PyTorch while the scanner misses the code-execution globals.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit f98f9bd89b16ab1b1b1b6366acddd1b2a4d36fe9 introduced old-format PyTorch scanning and, in the same focused commit, created src/picklescan/torch.py:get_magic_number with the literal INT/LONG-opcode heuristic and src/picklescan/scanner.py:scan_pytorch with the pre-scan magic-number rejection. Its immediate parent had neither torch.py nor scan_pytorch, so this is the smallest original commit that wrote the flawed semantic approximation; later cursor, exception-handling, routing, and logging changes retained rather than originated it.

The advisory declares affected versions <1.0.3 and patched version 1.0.3.

A targeted standard-library reproduction of the first pickle produced opcodes PROTO, GLOBAL, BINPUT, BINUNICODE, BINPUT, TUPLE1, BINPUT, REDUCE, BINPUT, STOP. audit_record.bug_semantics: A pickle GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL for the module-level callable profile.run is parsed as module="profile", name="run". PickleScan classified a global as an issue only when the module appeared in its manually enumerated unsafe map and the extracted name exactly matched that module's filter (or the filter was "*"). The original map omitted profile entirely; a later attempted hardening used {"Profile.run", "Profile.runctx"}, which still could not match the extracted module-level names "run" and "runctx". Thus a malicious pickle could produce zero issues and then profile.run(statement) would reach Profile.run and exec(statement) when unpickled.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The flaw originated in the first PickleScan implementation: it introduced an exact-name, manually enumerated dangerous-global filter without any entry for Python's profile module. That made profile.run executable but undetected from the scanner's first release lineage. Commit aecd11be98702caa9ba9b12189d91ad596a36114 later added class-qualified profile names, but it was not the BIC because its immediate parent already allowed the same module-level profile.run payload; it only preserved the pre-existing omission as a name-shape mismatch.

review_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated or otherwise protocol-reachable Kyuubi client can supply a local-file URI in Spark path-bearing session/batch configuration. When kyuubi.session.local.dir.allow.list is nonempty, the server accepted the URI whenever the unnormalized uri.getPath string began with an allowed directory. An absolute path such as /allowed/../outside/secret therefore passes the textual startsWith check, but the downstream filesystem/Spark consumer resolves .. and uses a local file outside the allow list. This bypass exposes server-local files to frontend clients.

audit_record.bug_semantics: ChaiScript's built-in async() launched a script closure with std::async(std::launch::async, ...) but did not make the Dispatch_Engine own or join the worker. During engine teardown, an outstanding script worker could continue formatting an eval_error and call Dispatch_Engine::get_type_name and Type_Info::bare_equal while the main thread destroyed the engine's type maps, producing a race-dependent heap use-after-free.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2 first registered async() in include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp as a bare std::async launch and returned only its future; it added no engine-lifetime tracking or teardown synchronization. That single addition created the vulnerable cross-thread lifetime relationship. Later edits only adjusted registration syntax, module passing, namespaces, or formatting while retaining the same untracked launch.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the BIC commit object names author Jason Turner <jason@emptycrate.com> and committer Jason Turner <jason@emptycrate.com>; its complete message is 'Add future support, and fix returning of r-values' and has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI trailer.
audit_record.evidence: First-party issue https://github.com/ChaiScript/ChaiScript/issues/636 documents the ASan UAF path: an async worker formatting eval_error calls include/chaiscript/dispatchkit/dispatchkit.hpp get_type_name and include/chaiscript/dispatchkit/type_info.hpp Type_Info::bare_equal after the main thread frees the type-map node; the maintainer closed it as fixed by PR https://github.com/ChaiScript/ChaiScript/pull/656. In the validated full-history clone, `git log -L 50,56:include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp 1b27d0dd15f45b4781273bc039713a8d8608cf86` follows the vulnerable std::async line through formatting/registration-only commits and ends at 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2. Narrow `git log --reverse -S 'std::async(std::launch::async' -- include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp` reports exactly the 2015 addition 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2 and the 2026 removal 7b95ff5126f0365c101b08fa33b50ae387342484. `git show 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2` shows the BIC adding future registration plus `async`, whose lambda directly returns `std::async(std::launch::async, t_func)`. Direct parent-tree inspection with `git show a32a180a063d9186ca38b2708a9c19d50da378db:include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp` shows the file exists but has neither <future>, future registration, async registration, nor std::async, proving immediate-parent absence. The BIC's own unittests/future.chai demonstrates four script functions launched through async(), confirming the feature's intended attack-relevant path. Version checks show v5.5.1 (commit 7478d5726425e725e1dd1a7c60f2059f55fab795) lacks the mechanism, v5.5.1..v5.6.0 contains the BIC, `git describe --contains` places it at tags/v5.6.0~12, and `git tag --contains` lists every release v5.6.0 through v6.1.0, matching the advisory's upper affected boundary. Fix commit 7b95ff5126f0365c101b08fa33b50ae387342484 is a one-parent direct source fix on develop after v6.1.0: it removes the raw std::async registration, makes Dispatch_Engine track spawned std::threads, and joins them in its destructor before shared state is destroyed; its regression test explicitly destroys an engine while async work remains. No release tag in the clone contains the fix, so the first patched boundary in public history is that develop commit rather than a tagged release. Finally, `git cat-file commit 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2` supplies the BIC-only identity/message evidence quoted in ai_marker.
audit_record.reasoning: The advisory's crashing instruction is Type_Info::bare_equal, but that comparison did not create the lifetime violation; it is merely where the async worker dereferenced already-freed engine-owned type data. The causal root is the first public async entry point that allowed engine-dependent script work to outlive engine storage. The -L trace distinguishes 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2 from later moves/refactors, while the -S result brackets the mechanism from its addition to the direct fix. The immediate parent contains the standard library without any future/async facility, whereas the BIC adds the untracked forced-async launch in one regular, non-squash commit; therefore it is the smallest real BIC and parent absence is directly proven. PR #656 fixes the same lifecycle defect by transferring thread ownership to Dispatch_Engine and joining before teardown, validating the causal choice. Although the fixing commit is explicitly AI-assisted, the protocol attributes AI only from the BIC commit object. The 2015 BIC has a human author and committer and no AI marker or trailer, so the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

review_record.bug_semantics: ChaiScript's built-in async() launched a std::async worker executing a script closure that could continue using its Dispatch_Engine after the owning ChaiScript instance began destruction. If that worker raised eval_error while the main thread destroyed the engine, error formatting called Dispatch_Engine::get_type_name and Type_Info::bare_equal over entries in the concurrently freed type map, producing the reported heap-use-after-free. The dereference in bare_equal is the observed sink, not the lifecycle root cause; the missing ownership/join relationship for engine-spawned workers is the flaw.
review_record.flaw_origin: Commit 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2 first registered the script-visible async function in include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp as a direct std::async(std::launch::async, t_func) call and returned only its future, without registering the spawned work with Dispatch_Engine or making engine destruction join it.

The maintainer closed it on 2026-04-11 with `Closed in #656`.

In the validated full-history clone, `git show 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2 -- include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp include/chaiscript/dispatchkit/bootstrap_stl.hpp` shows the first addition of <future>, future bindings, and `std::async(std::launch::async, t_func)` under the script name `async`. `git log -L 51,54:include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp 1b27d0dd15f45b4781273bc039713a8d8608cf86` follows that same registration through formatting/refactor-only edits back to 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2; repository-wide `git log --all -S 'std::async' -- .` independently includes that origin.

audit_record.bug_semantics: A script-controlled integer zero reaches Boxed_Number::go in the assign_remainder arm. The vulnerable arm executes *t_lhs %= c_rhs without check_divide_by_zero(c_rhs), so integer remainder assignment by zero raises SIGFPE and can terminate the embedding process rather than raising ChaiScript's arithmetic error.

primary_record.bug_semantics: When locally supplied ChaiScript executes integer compound remainder with a zero right-hand operand (for example, `ret %= 0`), `Boxed_Number::go` dispatches to `Operators::Opers::assign_remainder` and performs native C++ integer `%=` without first calling `check_divide_by_zero`. The processor therefore raises SIGFPE and can terminate the embedding process instead of producing ChaiScript's arithmetic error.

review_record.bug_semantics: A script-controlled integer right operand reaches Boxed_Number::go for assign_remainder. review_record.bug_semantics: In the barbuk theme's default python_venv segment, when neither CONDA_DEFAULT_ENV nor VIRTUAL_ENV_PROMPT is set and the current directory contains pyproject.toml, awk extracts the quoted requires-python value without filtering. __python_venv_prompt echoes that attacker-controlled value; __prompt-command captures the segment output and appends it directly to PS1. Thus a victim using the barbuk theme who cd's into an attacker-prepared directory emits embedded raw OSC/CSI/control bytes to the terminal on every prompt render, allowing terminal escape-sequence injection.

Its direct parent 8417414a15ca085a05d4822e65e7bbbd48876e72 still only handled active Conda/virtualenv state and had no pyproject.toml/requires-python path.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The authenticated Alertmanager and Prometheus proxy controllers called skip_forgery_protection while forwarding the browser-controlled method, path, query, and (for Alertmanager) body to their upstream services. A cross-site page could therefore cause a logged-in browser to send its ambient Upright session to a proxy action and reach an enabled upstream write or management endpoint, including Alertmanager silence creation or Prometheus /-/reload, without a Rails authenticity token or an equivalent provenance check.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable proxy implementation originated before the available public Git history. Public commit dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa added both already-vulnerable controllers in a commit explicitly titled 'Move UI and Traceroute probe to engine'; the repository itself begins with an 'Initial extraction', and the project's first-party launch article says Upright started as an internal tool. Because a move is not a BIC, the commit that originally chose skip_forgery_protection for session-authenticated, general-purpose upstream proxies is not present in this clone.
audit_record.ai_marker: unavailable (not absent): the original BIC commit object is outside the public basecamp/upright history, so its author, committer, and trailers cannot be inspected; no AI judgment is inferred from the later extraction/move commit

Origin trace: git log -L '/skip_forgery_protection/',+1 on each file at the advisory snapshot reaches 29b423ea9e0cec753da97105afccf7a694a5b0e6 ('Continue extraction of Upright core', a namespace-only rewrite) and then dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa ('Move UI and Traceroute probe to engine'), where both files appear from /dev/null already containing the skip and forwarding mechanism. Direct parent-tree check shows dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa^ is 2a7dfaf0f5411a0195d11c426aeeab8f34a70211 and git ls-tree -r of that parent has neither proxy controller; this proves absence in the public parent but does not make a stated move the original BIC. git rev-list --max-parents=0 yields 7b400a7d44db470a00634e950012af3157ab0795, titled 'Initial extraction'. The first-party article https://dev.37signals.com/introducing-upright/ states that Upright started as an internal tool before it was open-sourced, corroborating the missing pre-extraction lineage. Fix lifecycle: af938dd148c3fa8d148c51fb664f4e34e6a8ef42 first added the CVE-specific Fetch-Metadata/Origin gate; c53258998efee82d69e64237ba7e362c4160a1c4 made missing provenance fail closed; subsequent review hardened the same-origin rule; d94dedb56cec78461cd14113c337034734813d58 removed skip_forgery_protection and retained Rails verification by overriding verified_request? only for a valid token, bearer token, or accepted same-origin provenance. The relevant controller/concern trees at d94dedb56cec78461cd14113c337034734813d58 and PR merge 997009a6778687ac8c1f0833f2850ea808742cce are identical; merge-base checks place d94dedb56cec78461cd14113c337034734813d58 in 997009a6778687ac8c1f0833f2850ea808742cce and that merge in origin/main. Version boundary: dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa is contained by tags v0.1.2, v0.2.0, and v0.3.0, while no tag contains d94dedb56cec78461cd14113c337034734813d58 or 997009a6778687ac8c1f0833f2850ea808742cce. RubyGems lists released 0.1.0, 0.1.2, 0.2.0, and 0.3.0; current lib/upright/version.rb remains 0.3.0 and CHANGELOG.md records CVE-2026-67990 under Unreleased. audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerable behavior is the combination of ambient session authentication, an explicit global CSRF skip on each metrics proxy, and unrestricted forwarding to upstream APIs; the advisory's cited snapshot demonstrates that complete attack path. Line-level history does not support treating the January public addition as causal authorship: both controllers arrive already formed in a commit whose stated operation is a move during a repository extraction, and the next commit only changes Ruby namespace syntax. The public parent lacks the files, but the root and first-party project history establish that this is a boundary created by open-sourcing an existing internal tool, not proof that dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa first wrote the flawed mechanism. Protocol therefore forbids selecting that move as the BIC. The remediation was developed as a sequence because the first provenance gate still allowed residual cases; d94dedb56cec78461cd14113c337034734813d58 is the final direct CSRF implementation whose relevant tree landed through 997009a6778687ac8c1f0833f2850ea808742cce. All release tags precede that landing, matching the Unreleased changelog and the advisory's absence of a released version range. Since the true BIC and its commit object are outside accessible public history, neither immediate-parent absence for the original write nor BIC-only AI authorship can be established. This is a genuine public-history boundary, so BLOCKED is required rather than NOT_AI or EVIDENCE_GAP.
audit_record.remaining_gap: The inaccessible pre-open-source/internal Git commit that first wrote the two session-authenticated proxy controllers with skip_forgery_protection, its immediate parent tree, and that BIC commit object's author/committer/trailers are required to complete causal and AI attribution; the public extraction begins after those facts already existed. No patched gem release is available yet, although the fix is present on origin/main.

review_record.bug_semantics: Upright exposed all-verbs Prometheus and Alertmanager proxy routes to session-authenticated browser users while both proxy controllers called skip_forgery_protection and forwarded the request method, path, and body to their upstream services. An unauthenticated attacker could induce a logged-in victim's browser to issue a cross-site request carrying the ambient session (including a Lax-cookie top-level GET) and reach enabled upstream write or management operations such as creating an Alertmanager silence or requesting Prometheus /-/reload; there was no Fetch-Metadata, Origin, or equivalent provenance gate.
review_record.flaw_origin: The public repository does not contain the true implementation origin. dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa first adds both skip_forgery_protection proxy controllers to this repository in a 58-file, 2,918-insertion commit explicitly titled 'Move UI and Traceroute probe to engine', but its routes do not expose them. 29b423ea9e0cec753da97105afccf7a694a5b0e6 later adds the all-verbs proxy routes and completes the reachable vulnerable chain in a 98-file, 3,427-insertion/1,905-deletion commit explicitly titled 'Continue extraction of Upright core'. Both are import/extraction aggregates rather than the smallest commit that originally designed the vulnerable proxy, and the pre-extraction source history is absent from this clone.
review_record.ai_marker: Unavailable for the true BIC because its commit object is outside the public history. As a non-BIC boundary check only, git cat-file commit on import commits dbf67daef2c624c1d5f01ef4233a8bccb3c927aa and 29b423ea9e0cec753da97105afccf7a694a5b0e6 shows author/committer Lewis Buckley <lewis@37signals.com>, SSH signatures, the subjects 'Move UI and Traceroute probe to engine' and 'Continue extraction of Upright core', and no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI attribution trailer. Those marker absences are not used to classify the unavailable true BIC.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The optimized constant-integer for-loop exposed its native stack-local counter to script code through var(&i). ChaiScript's intentional := reference assignment could copy that alias into a returned Boxed_Value, including one transported by async/future. When the optimized-loop lambda returned, the counter's lifetime ended, but the escaped value retained its raw pointer; later numeric conversion in Boxed_Number::get_as dereferenced the dangling storage, producing garbage, an invalid read, or a segmentation fault.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 683164650a462b6d5ea58bb899f4c2e668243a1d first added the compiled standard-for-loop path and the causal pair `int i = for_loop_params.start;` / `t_ss.add_object(for_loop_params.id, var(&i));`. Its parent used the ordinary For_AST_Node path and had neither statement. primary_record.bug_semantics: The optimized standard integer for-loop exposed its stack-local C++ counter to ChaiScript with var(&i). ChaiScript's intentional := reference-assignment could therefore copy an alias to that counter into a returned Boxed_Value. audit_record.bug_semantics: ChaiScript evaluated user-defined function bodies through ordinary native C++ recursion without enforcing a maximum ChaiScript call depth. A script-defined operator can re-enter itself from a ${...} string-interpolation expression, repeatedly traversing function dispatch and AST evaluation until the process exhausts its native stack and terminates with stack overflow/SIGSEGV instead of raising a recoverable script or host exception.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The omission originates in 8f89e446087be57559cda289c342ee9227cb7140, the first commit that made parsed ChaiScript function definitions executable: wesley/main.cpp added eval_function0 through eval_function3, each directly re-evaluating the stored function-body AST via eval_token, and registered those callbacks from the Function_Def evaluator with no recursion-depth check. Later commits completed dispatch, added string interpolation, introduced call_depth bookkeeping, and moved/refactored the evaluator, but those changes did not first create the underlying unbounded recursive script-call mechanism.

review_record.bug_semantics: ChaiScript accepted recursively re-entering user-defined script functions without any maximum call-depth check. The disclosed script defines string::`/=` so its body evaluates `${this/= 2}`, immediately dispatching the same operator again; eval_function and AST_Node_Impl::eval repeatedly enter Function_Push_Pop/new_function_call until the native thread stack is exhausted and the host aborts with stack-overflow/SIGSEGV.
