review_record.bug_semantics: ChaiScript's script-visible async() launched a callable with std::async(std::launch::async, ...) but the ChaiScript/Dispatch_Engine did not own or join the resulting worker. A script could start asynchronous work and finish while that work was still resolving identifiers. Engine teardown on the main thread then freed shared Dispatch_Engine state, including map nodes in the symbol/object tables, while a worker still used that state. A subsequent heterogeneous std::map lookup read a freed std::string key through chaiscript::str_less::operator(), producing the reported heap-use-after-free. str_less is the observed ASan crash site, not the causal ownership defect. The issue #632 PoC launches two async functions that repeatedly access undefined re6 and then lets the script end without waiting for the futures, creating the teardown/read race.
review_record.flaw_origin: The smallest true BIC is 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2, which first added future support and registered script async() as a direct std::async(std::launch::async, t_func) call in include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp without engine lifetime tracking or a teardown join. Its sole parent a32a180a063d9186ca38b2708a9c19d50da378db has no <future> include, future type, async registration, or std::async launch. Later commits 630c618ae7d87bd7bee7979997f31bad7fecd803, 5ff97979fd85db218112f0a69d21fe2f95ef9abc, 7ab6bce7faf0ba466b38a9ed31ccbdadbbd99ecd, 70cdbef69333a5fecd6e9e034d9e1428a544c8a5, and cff6a0acedbc1b8e53aeef118570929b50a711c9 only adjusted wrapping/module APIs or formatting around the already-vulnerable launch and are not introducers.

review_record.bug_semantics: A remote unauthenticated attacker can submit an unlimited sequence of incorrect administrator credentials to either /j_security_check (j_password) or /management/domain (HTTP Authorization). Before the fix, each request is authenticated immediately and a failed attempt merely returns the login error/HTTP 401; no per-user/host attempt state, delay, concurrency cap, or temporary lockout makes online brute-force guessing progressively more expensive.
review_record.flaw_origin: The smallest causal origin recoverable from public history is javaee/glassfish commit 0fee8143d3ad099bb7b4583785693957c838523a (SVN r29730), which added the REST wrapper and its security path for /management/domain. RestAdapter.authenticate invokes AdminAuthenticator for every request and, on false, immediately emits 401 plus WWW-Authenticate: BASIC without retaining failed-attempt state. Its parent exposed /management/domain directly and had no authenticated failed-login path. Commit c1f1b2942b2a657eb61e707069dd4ea9d3e3a730 later expanded the same omission to the Admin Console: AdminConsoleAuthModule accepted /j_security_check credentials and posted them to REST, forwarding failure to the error page without throttling. Eclipse commit 571714739b23e16c4c90d5229b806433920b3bcb is only the 2018 Initial Contribution snapshot; following the files in the public predecessor history decomposes that aggregate to 0fee8143d3ad099bb7b4583785693957c838523a rather than treating the import or later moves as the BIC.

The updated Eclipse CVE publication request https://gitlab.eclipse.org/security/cve-assignment/-/issues/128 gives the complete affected set: 5.1.0; 6.0.0 through 6.2.5; 7.0.0 through 7.0.25; 7.1.0; and 8.0.0 through versions before 8.0.3. Later authenticator rewrites, module moves, the 2018 Eclipse snapshot import, and the 2026 merge are not introducers. audit_record.bug_semantics: Genkit's unauthenticated developer servers listened beyond a loopback-only trust boundary and did not validate the HTTP Host header. A LAN peer, or a website using DNS rebinding, could reach the Tools/Dev UI or reflection runAction handler, execute registered actions with attacker-controlled input and context, and read results. The telemetry trace SSE handler also set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, exposing trace data. CORS was not an authorization gate because it did not prevent handler execution and DNS rebinding made the request same-origin to the attacker's page.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The earliest public carrier is squash aggregate 91ed3de52e7db92943886526395ad8eac6faa77f. Its parent 805600159f34ca96d95c26c10c7b2799cb5951ce had only the stub Runner server and no runAction or reflection execution path; the aggregate adds an unauthenticated Runner runAction proxy, a reflection /api/runAction executor, and listeners without host arguments or Host validation. The aggregate message enumerates 27 squashed member changes, including 'Added basic Reflection API', 'Added starting of app code when starting Runner API', and 'Implemented passthrough endpoints in Runner API'. Those unavailable member objects must be distinguished to identify the smallest commit that first completed the exploitable path, so the aggregate itself is not accepted as the BIC.

primary_record.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated Genkit developer Tools server accepted action-execution requests while listening beyond a loopback-only trust boundary and did not validate the HTTP Host header. CORS only controls which origins receive browser-readable response headers; it does not stop the handler, and a DNS-rebound page retains its attacker origin while resolving its hostname to the developer machine. Consequently a LAN client or DNS-rebound browser could reach the action runner, supply an action key and input (later also context), execute any registered flow/tool/model/prompt, and read the returned result. The reported chain also used the telemetry SSE endpoint's wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin to read trace inputs and outputs.
primary_record.flaw_origin: The earliest persisted tree that makes the network-listening Runner API actually execute actions is squash aggregate 91ed3de52e7db92943886526395ad8eac6faa77f: it adds genkit-tools/src/runner/router.ts with a runAction mutation that proxies to the reflection server and changes genkit-tools/src/runner/runner.ts to expose that router through api.listen(port) without a host argument or Host validation. review_record.bug_semantics: Genkit's unauthenticated developer servers accepted requests on non-loopback interfaces without validating the HTTP Host header. audit_record.bug_semantics: Command_OPEN_POWERSHELL took the directory of the file being edited and interpolated it verbatim into the PowerShell program -NoExit -Command "Set-Location -Path '<directory>'". A Windows directory name may contain a single quote, so an attacker-controlled directory can terminate the PowerShell single-quoted literal and append PowerShell statements. When a victim opens a file from that directory and invokes Open PowerShell/Open Terminal (including the administrator variant), ShellExecuteW starts powershell.exe and executes the injected statements with the victim's privileges.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 3340e0d352a795ddfaf89214e66f7989371b21c7 converted the existing Command_OPEN_POWERSHELL scaffold from a cmd.exe invocation to powershell.exe and first added the vulnerable Set-Location command template using strFolder.c_str() without PowerShell single-quote escaping. Its immediate parent still constructed a cmd.exe '/k cd /d' command and had neither the PowerShell Set-Location template nor the vulnerable single-quoted interpolation.

evidence: First-party lifecycle: https://jvn.jp/en/jp/JVN74538868/ identifies CVE-2026-59561/CWE-78, says the current-directory string is not neutralized, describes the crafted-directory -> victim opens file -> Open Terminal -> arbitrary-command path, and sets the patched product boundary at v2.4.3. The repository advisory https://github.com/sakura-editor/sakura/security/advisories/GHSA-6x2x-729r-wjh5 specifically names Open PowerShell and Open PowerShell as Administrator; https://github.com/sakura-editor/sakura/releases/tag/v2.4.3 lists the corresponding security fix.

This non-merge, single-parent commit wrote the unsafe language boundary itself; the later merge c18e549fcb7c877bf57287cea857a6ef7d49898b merely aggregated the visible feature commits.

Subsequent commits in that line history change comments/types/refactoring but retain the same unescaped strFolder template until the security fix, so neither the later merge nor the 2025 file move is the BIC.

Immediate-parent absence: `git cat-file -p 3340e0d352a795ddfaf89214e66f7989371b21c7` gives sole parent de6749296b8b9a3ffa2c281d26758770a956f31a. Thus the advisory's vulnerable PowerShell interpolation is absent from the immediate parent tree.

Exploitability follows the parser boundary visible in the BIC: strFolder is derived from the opened document path, and a directory component such as `name'; <attacker-statement>; '` closes the quoted -Path value. PowerShell then parses the appended statement because the whole interpolated value is supplied as executable `-Command` text, rather than as an opaque working-directory argument.

Because an apostrophe in a Windows directory name was not escaped, a crafted path such as C:\safe'; Start-Process calc; #' terminates the string and appends attacker-chosen PowerShell. A victim need only open a file from that directory and invoke Open PowerShell or Open PowerShell as Administrator; the latter can execute after the UAC flow with elevated rights.
review_record.flaw_origin: Atomic commit 3340e0d352a795ddfaf89214e66f7989371b21c7 changed the pre-existing PowerShell-command skeleton from a cmd.exe /k cd invocation to powershell.exe with `-NoExit -Command "Set-Location -Path '%s'"`, passing strFolder.c_str() without PowerShell single-quote escaping. That exact semantic conversion first created the injection; the immediately preceding skeleton commit still invoked cmd.exe and therefore did not contain this PowerShell parsing flaw.

The server trusted the packet's attacker-controlled downstream configuration, policies, credentials, and transport target, registered a connector, and deployed an outbound Core federation connection without checking the connection Subject or any federation-deployment role. audit_record.bug_semantics: RustCrypto ml-dsa signature decoding reused one monotonicity predicate for two encodings with different rules. Hint cut offsets may repeat because a polynomial may have no hints, but hint indices inside each polynomial must be strictly increasing. Changing the shared comparison from < to <= made repeated cuts valid while also accepting duplicate indices. Verification could therefore accept a non-canonical, byte-distinct signature carrying a repeated hint index, causing ML-DSA signature malleability across ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65, and ML-DSA-87.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The assigned c2sp/wycheproof repository supplies detecting conformance vectors, not the vulnerable verifier. The flaw originated in RustCrypto/signatures PR #895. Its first member commit 92d2a8211581610191ee489372231aa644760c1a directly changed ml-dsa/src/hint.rs from strict < to non-strict <=; later PR members did not first write that condition. The five-member PR was squash-merged to mainline as b01c3b73dd08d0094e089aa234f78b6089ec1f38, whose tree matches the final PR member, so the squash carrier is not the smallest real BIC.

primary_record.bug_semantics: RustCrypto ml-dsa signature decoding used one monotonic() predicate for two different encodings. Hint cut offsets may repeat because an ML-DSA polynomial may contain no hints, but hint indices within each polynomial must be strictly increasing. Changing the shared predicate from < to <= made cuts valid but also accepted equal adjacent indices. A verifier therefore decoded a non-canonical signature containing a repeated hint index and could accept a byte-distinct malleation of a valid signature.

audit_record.bug_semantics: An authenticated board editor could send a single-block or batch PATCH naming a comment block created by another member. The handlers checked only the caller's general ability to manage board cards and the target block's board, then applied the caller-controlled patch; they never enforced comment ownership or the elevated permission for acting on other users' comments. This let an editor alter another member's comment and caused unauthorized integrity loss.

review_record.bug_semantics: Before the fix, both PATCH /boards/{boardID}/blocks/{blockID} and the batch PATCH /boards/{boardID}/blocks endpoint treated a comment as an ordinary board block. An authenticated user with board-wide PermissionManageBoardCards (the editor capability) could name a comment created by another member and alter its title/fields: the handlers checked board access/association but did not compare block.CreatedBy with the session user or require the elevated PermissionDeleteOthersComments capability. The single endpoint then called PatchBlockAndNotify and the batch endpoint called PatchBlocksAndNotify, so the unauthorized patch reached persistent storage. The fix loads each target and, for TypeComment with CreatedBy != userID, rejects the request unless PermissionDeleteOthersComments is present; it also preserves the original creator/create time in the insert/history path.
review_record.flaw_origin: The smallest reconstructable BIC is PR #877 member 7c1d63a9d9ee6a5f82655f780196d96f35cdd12e ('Adding support for patch blocks'), not the mainline squash c734cfb8d16b1a4a20e3fb03b3afdf052fa53fce. That member first registered a session-authenticated PATCH-by-block-ID route and implemented handlePatchBlock as getContainer -> decode arbitrary BlockPatch -> App.PatchBlock, without loading the target for a comment-owner authorization decision. Its parent already supported the 'comment' block type and rendered comments, but had no PATCH route or handlePatchBlock. Later 3450eb6d4ffda75d303f53795b3d7c38cecd2330 added the batch variant; aa540e73ce669a1acd491a5edd7d55199ef1b87c converted the guard to board-wide PermissionManageBoardCards while retaining the missing object-owner check; c1f2ae63165dfc5a162b6d364c3f1644e5114a1c only moved the handler to server/api/blocks.go. The October 2025 deletion fix 80c4012a52f3d59ef38ddde90f12cb761b33caa6 protected deletion of others' comments but left modification exposed.

audit_record.bug_semantics: A STOMP client authenticated with only SEND or CONSUME permission could request a routing type that an existing address did not support. STOMP's auto-create path added that routing type by calling the broker server's updateAddressInfo directly, without the ServerSession CREATE_ADDRESS authorization check; the subsequent routing-semantics check then observed the newly added type and accepted the send or subscription. This let a low-privilege user mutate address routing configuration despite lacking createAddress permission.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 added the first existing-address/missing-routing-type branch to StompConnection.autoCreateDestinationIfPossible. It copied the address's routing types, added the client-requested effectiveAddressRoutingType, and invoked manager.getServer().updateAddressInfo(...) directly. The parent only auto-created through the authenticated ServerSession when an address did not exist and otherwise left an unsupported routing type for checkRoutingSemantics to reject. Later edits moved or modernized the same sink but did not originate the authorization bypass.

audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerability is the authorization bypass in the existing-address routing-type augmentation, not generic STOMP auto-creation. Before the BIC, STOMP could auto-create a missing address through ServerSession (and its security boundary), but it did not mutate an existing address to satisfy a mismatched routing type; checkRoutingSemantics rejected that request. ARTEMIS-1794 commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 deliberately enabled two STOMP routing types on the same address and introduced the smallest causal branch: it directly changed the broker's AddressInfo outside ServerSession authorization. The exact sink is absent from its immediate parent and is present beginning with release 2.6.0. Later refactors retain the same mechanism, so they are not introducers. ARTEMIS-5996 commit 53173375c4d5e4b57890e89d37ed8b666c974474 is the direct fix: it deletes the duplicated STOMP mutation logic and sends both attack paths through ServerSession.checkAutoCreate, whose createAddress path enforces CREATE_ADDRESS; its regression tests cover both send-only and consume-only credentials, and it lands in the first patched tag 2.54.0 after the sink remains in 2.53.0. Although the advisory conservatively lists versions back to 2.0.0, tag-level code establishes that this exact flaw begins in 2.6.0. Finally, the BIC commit object has no AI authorship or generation marker, so the causal result is NOT_AI.

review_record.bug_semantics: When STOMP auto-create is enabled, an authenticated principal holding only SEND or CONSUME permission can request an unsupported routing type in a SEND destination-type or SUBSCRIBE subscription-type header. The vulnerable STOMP path sees the existing address, copies its routing-type set, adds the requested type, and calls ActiveMQServer.updateAddressInfo directly, bypassing the ServerSession CREATE_ADDRESS security check. Because checkRoutingSemantics runs only after this mutation, it sees the newly added type and accepts the operation. The result is an unauthorized persistent augmentation of the address routing semantics.
review_record.flaw_origin: Commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 intentionally added support for STOMP clients to use the same address with different routing types. Its new existing-address branch performed the update through manager.getServer().updateAddressInfo rather than the authorization-enforcing ServerSession API, creating the root authorization bypass.
review_record.ai_marker: None. `git cat-file commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69` shows author Justin Bertram <jbertram@apache.org>, committer Clebert Suconic <clebertsuconic@apache.org>, the subject `ARTEMIS-1794 STOMP clients using same addr w/diff routing types`, an empty body, and no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, AI, or bot marker. The BIC is an ordinary one-parent human commit from 2018.
evidence: The Apache oss-security announcement at https://www.openwall.com/lists/oss-security/2026/05/27/8 identifies ARTEMIS-5996/CVE-2026-40914, describes unauthorized routing-type augmentation by a STOMP user with only send or consume permission, declares 2.0.0-2.44.0 and 2.50.0-2.53.0 affected, and recommends 2.54.0.

`git show d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 -- artemis-protocols/artemis-stomp-protocol/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/artemis/core/protocol/stomp/StompConnection.java` shows the first existing-address branch: when the requested type is absent and auto-create-addresses is enabled, it copies existing types, adds the requested type, and invokes `manager.getServer().updateAddressInfo(simpleQueue, routingTypes)`. The same commit's tests explicitly say a STOMP send should alter an existing address to support the second routing type.

At the BIC, `git grep -n -E 'autoCreateDestinationIfPossible|checkRoutingSemantics' d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 -- .../StompConnection.java .../VersionedStompFrameHandler.java` shows mutation before validation on both paths: subscribe lines 692/694 and send lines 190/192 call autoCreateDestinationIfPossible before checkRoutingSemantics.

Direct parent verification: `git show e937c9903f9fa429c23fe50a3fd49e99ad2de0b9:artemis-protocols/artemis-stomp-protocol/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/artemis/core/protocol/stomp/StompConnection.java` shows autoCreateDestinationIfPossible acts only when getAddressInfo is null, creates through `session.createAddress`, and contains no existing-address routing-set update. Its subsequent checkRoutingSemantics rejects a requested type absent from an existing address.

Independent origin checks agree: `git log 53173375c4d5e4b57890e89d37ed8b666c974474^ -L '/public void autoCreateDestinationIfPossible/,/^   }/':artemis-protocols/artemis-stomp-protocol/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/artemis/core/protocol/stomp/StompConnection.java` traces the vulnerable branch to d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69; `git log --all --reverse -S'manager.getServer().updateAddressInfo(simpleQueue, routingTypes)' -- .../StompConnection.java` returns d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 as the addition and ede2051960ddd6bf5657076fe5889f18a5699c6c only as a later refactor/removal of that spelling.

Release introduction: tag 2.5.0 resolves to 5f5b1dcf8f731b53d1b271fdde46dddacdd71bd7 and has no `updateAddressInfo(simpleQueue, routingTypes)` hit; tag 2.6.0 resolves to bcaa11c2eea681d5758398be0b8c2ff8ae2c2878 and contains it at StompConnection.java:297. `git tag --contains d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69` begins at 2.6.0 and includes every existing release tag through 2.44.0 and then 2.50.0 onward. Thus direct history narrows the exact mechanism's effective floor to 2.6.0, despite the advisory's conservative 2.0.0 floor; no 2.45.0-2.49.0 tags exist.

Closing fix: `git show 53173375c4d5e4b57890e89d37ed8b666c974474` deletes the duplicated direct update and changes both SEND and SUBSCRIBE to StompConnection.checkAutoCreate, which calls `getSession().getCoreSession().checkAutoCreate(QueueConfiguration...)`. In tag 2.54.0, ServerSessionImpl.checkAutoCreate updates an existing address by calling ServerSessionImpl.createAddress, whose line `securityCheck(art.getName(), CheckType.CREATE_ADDRESS, this)` enforces the missing permission.

Fix boundary: `git grep -n -E 'updateAddressInfo\(simpleDestination|checkAutoCreate\(destination' 2.53.0 -- .../StompConnection.java .../VersionedStompFrameHandler.java` finds the vulnerable direct update at StompConnection.java:197. The same command at 2.54.0 finds checkAutoCreate at StompConnection.java:491 and VersionedStompFrameHandler.java:196 and no direct update. `git tag --contains 53173375c4d5e4b57890e89d37ed8b666c974474` returns 2.54.0, 2.55.0, and 2.56.0, making 2.54.0 the first fixed release.

`git cat-file commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69` directly verifies the full parent e937c9903f9fa429c23fe50a3fd49e99ad2de0b9, human author/committer identities, 2018 timestamps, and complete absence of AI trailers or bot identity. The commit has one parent and is the narrow ARTEMIS-1794 implementation, not a merge, release/backport, revert, move, or squash aggregate.
review_record.reasoning: The vulnerability is caused by the newly added direct server update, not by later renames or refactors. The parent cannot mutate an existing address and instead rejects a mismatched requested routing type, while d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 adds exactly the mutation that makes the later semantic check self-satisfying. The direct fix 53173375c4d5e4b57890e89d37ed8b666c974474 removes that bypass and delegates to a session path that checks CREATE_ADDRESS. Tag and source checks establish introduction in 2.6.0, persistence through 2.53.0, and closure in 2.54.0; the published lower bound of 2.0.0 is broader than the exact code history. AI attribution is judged solely from the BIC object. It contains only named human identities and no AI/bot marker, so reporter credit to bugbunny.ai and any properties of the 2026 fix are irrelevant and the correct verdict is NOT_AI.

audit_record.bug_semantics: With address auto-creation disabled, an authenticated OpenWire client could request a non-durable JMS topic subscription on a nonexistent address while permitted to create and consume from the subscription queue but denied CREATE_ADDRESS. The topic path skipped the broker's address auto-creation preflight and directly created a temporary queue, which implicitly materialized the missing temporary address without enforcing CREATE_ADDRESS; the address remained until the OpenWire connection closed. The fix's regression fixture grants CREATE_NON_DURABLE_QUEUE, although the advisory prose calls the relevant permission createDurableQueue.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 84e8a87325a976c9970b8e85d03fc33207623af3 introduced Artemis's independent CREATE_ADDRESS permission and explicit separately-authorized address-creation operation while leaving the OpenWire non-durable-topic path able to create a temporary queue directly and the server queue-creation path able to materialize its missing address after checking only queue-creation permission. The older OpenWire code was a precursor, but before this commit there was no separate create-address authorization invariant for it to bypass.

audit_record.evidence: The bundle advisory defines an Incorrect Authorization flaw specifically in terms of a user lacking createAddress and gives affected boundaries Apache ActiveMQ Artemis 2.0.0-2.44.0 and Apache Artemis 2.50.0-2.52.0, fixed in 2.53.0. The disputed primary chose upstream HornetQ d0dbe869b803e17785afe6331c024d2fa7fe5d68 with parent 62f4810cde2af914db4549514a8d5ea80d6591ce because it first wrote the direct OpenWire topic/temporary-queue path; the reviewer chose 84e8a87325a976c9970b8e85d03fc33207623af3 with parent 0bcde8140fb1f0927de58fcf856f3b449a2cdf5d because that is when the independent address permission came into existence. Re-running `git log --reverse -S'CREATE_ADDRESS' -- artemis-server/src/main/java/org/apache/activemq/artemis/core/security/CheckType.java` returns 84e8a87325a976c9970b8e85d03fc33207623af3 as the first addition. primary_record.bug_semantics: With address auto-creation disabled, an authenticated OpenWire client could request a non-durable JMS topic subscription on a nonexistent address while holding the queue-creation and consume permissions sufficient for the subscription but lacking CREATE_ADDRESS/createAddress permission. The 2.53.0 regression test grants CREATE_NON_DURABLE_QUEUE (the advisory prose calls the relevant permission createDurableQueue). The OpenWire topic path created a temporary subscription queue directly; that temporary queue creation also materialized the missing temporary address without the topic path first enforcing the address-existence/CREATE_ADDRESS check. The unauthorized address lived until the OpenWire connection closed.
primary_record.flaw_origin: The original OpenWire consumer implementation sent topic subscriptions straight from AMQSession.createConsumer into AMQConsumer.init, where the non-durable branch generated a UUID queue name and called coreSession.createQueue(address, subQueueName, selector, true, false). Unlike the queue-destination branch added later, the topic branch never called the broker's auto-create preflight. In the affected implementation this mattered because ServerSessionImpl.createQueue conditioned its CREATE_ADDRESS security check on autoCreateAddresses, while ActiveMQServerImpl.createQueue separately materialized a missing address whenever the QueueConfiguration was temporary. Thus direct temporary queue creation could create its missing address with autoCreateAddresses=false, and the user's non-durable-queue permission reached implicit address creation without the required address permission.

audit_record.bug_semantics: Bastillion's authentication filter was mapped only to /manage/* and /admin/*, while the lmvc controller dispatcher accepted any raw request URI containing an annotated controller path plus .ktrl. A request such as /anything/manage/viewUsers.ktrl therefore missed the prefix-scoped AuthFilter but was still substring-dispatched to the privileged /manage/viewUsers controller; unauthenticated attackers could read administrative data, create a MANAGER account, and register systems.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The flawed routing primitive was first written in the lmvc framework's 2018 initial source commit: BaseKontroller.execute() used request.getRequestURI().contains(c.path() + DispatcherServlet.CTR_EXT). Bastillion first integrated that framework in 65475902748be6b86a95d17b8409518697fe1e77 while retaining prefix-only AuthFilter mappings, making the mismatch exploitable in the application. Later package renames, artifact releases, and the 2026 source import merely carried the same line forward.

audit_record.bug_semantics: When the image proxy is enabled, an authenticated forum user can embed an attacker-selected non-HTTPS URL in an IMG BBCode tag. SMF rewrites it to its own proxy.php URL and supplies the secret-derived hash, after which the server dereferences the selected URL. The hash therefore did not prevent an authenticated poster from causing SSRF into services visible to the SMF host.

primary_record.bug_semantics: When the image proxy is enabled, an authenticated poster can place an attacker-chosen non-HTTPS URL in a BBCode [img] tag. SMF's BBCode renderer converts that URL into a local proxy.php URL and generates the required secret-derived hash itself. A subsequent request to that local URL makes the forum server fetch the remote URL. Before the fixes, the fetch path did not resolve and reject private, loopback, link-local, or other reserved destination addresses on the initial request and every redirect, so an attacker-controlled hostname or redirect could make SMF request internal services, including link-local metadata endpoints.
primary_record.flaw_origin: The proxy fetch endpoint was already present in the immediate parent and required a secret-derived hash, but was not yet an attacker-usable signing oracle. Commit a892a53ba45330d69b8ad8b1ede82aebaa29537b completed the vulnerable mechanism by adding BBCode-renderer code that accepts the untrusted image URL and automatically emits /proxy.php?request=<url>&hash=md5(<url>.<secret>) without any destination-address validation. This is the smallest commit that made the pre-existing unvalidated server-side fetch reachable with a valid signature from attacker-controlled BBCode.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The attachment-approval path obtains the boards on which the authenticated user has approve_posts permission, but its per-attachment authorization predicate uses assignment rather than comparison: in 2.1, `$allowed_boards = array(0) || in_array(...)`, and in 3.0, `$allowed_boards = [0] || \in_array(...)`. Because `||` binds more tightly than `=`, the non-empty array on the left of `||` is truthy, the membership test is short-circuited, and boolean true is assigned to `$allowed_boards`; every queried pending attachment therefore passes the guard. A low-privileged authenticated user can approve, reject, or delete pending attachments on boards where that user lacks approve_posts.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable predicate predates the repository's accessible Git history. `git log -L 1799,1799:Sources/ManageAttachments.php c33589c13f9cfff339d2fe6874dcf6b8f15f643b` reaches only the sole root a18e888838460a816fdbc2703e7e05ce7f626c91 and shows the flawed line added from /dev/null at original line 1500. review_record.bug_semantics: The attachment-approval action accepts an authenticated request after a GET-session check, collects pending attachment IDs from either sa=all plus mid or a caller-supplied aid, obtains the boards on which the user has approve_posts, and then is supposed to retain only attachments whose message board is authorized. The condition uses assignment rather than comparison: in 2.1, `if ($allowed_boards = array(0) || in_array(...))`, and in 3.0, `if ($allowed_boards = [0] || \in_array(...))`. Because assignment has lower precedence than `||` and the non-empty `[0]`/`array(0)` operand is truthy, the right-hand boolean expression is always true, true is assigned to $allowed_boards, and every queried pending attachment passes. A low-privileged authenticated user with a valid session can consequently approve pending attachments without approve_posts, use reject to delete pending attachments, bypass moderation for the user's own uploads, and target or enumerate other users' pending attachment IDs across boards.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The reported mechanism is that POST /api/v1/invitation-code/redeem has no DeveloperDep or API-key dependency and treats an eight-character invitation code as the sole credential; a valid, unexpired, unredeemed code is looked up and exchanged for an SDK-scoped access JWT, a refresh token, and the bound user_id. Thus anyone who obtains a still-valid code can redeem it first. This is not actually missing authentication: the code was deliberately designed as a single-use bearer credential for standalone/mobile onboarding, and the CNA ultimately rejected CVE-2026-78154 as a false positive.

review_record.bug_semantics: The advisory characterizes POST /api/v1/invitation-code/redeem as missing authentication because it accepts only an invitation code and returns SDK access and refresh tokens. The first-party design makes the single-use invitation code itself a bearer credential: an authenticated developer generates a code bound server-side to a user, and the standalone mobile app redeems that secret without a second credential. The client cannot choose a user_id at redemption. The implemented code is eight characters sampled with secrets.choice from a 32-character alphabet (32^8 about 1.1 trillion possibilities), expires after seven days, is single-use, and later active codes are revoked when replaced. Redeemed access tokens carry scope sdk. audit_record.bug_semantics: On an installation whose active cluster credential was the compiled-in default, any network client that copied the public source constant into X-WolfStack-Secret passed require_auth() as the synthetic cluster-node principal without a session, API key, or user account. That principal could call management endpoints, including POST /api/containers/{runtime}/{id}/exec, which passed attacker-controlled command text to sh -c inside the selected Docker or LXC container as root.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 2d2d371527bde1e9d72eadcd2ee3e7c0ee3adfbc replaced the parent implementation's per-node, randomly generated /etc/wolfstack/cluster.key with one source-published CLUSTER_SECRET shared by every installation and made load_cluster_secret() return that constant. The pre-existing request gate compared X-WolfStack-Secret with state.cluster_secret without any source-address or recorded-peer check, so this replacement converted possession of public source text into authentication.

At the BIC tree, src/api/mod.rs require_auth() reads X-WolfStack-Secret, compares it against state.cluster_secret, and returns cluster-node on equality, with no peer/source check. At v25.9.1, src/api/mod.rs:7144-7153 shows POST /api/containers/{runtime}/{id}/exec guarded only by require_auth() before invoking sh -c with the supplied command.

Lifecycle history explains but does not replace the BIC: c8e3c7f08ba3c4a172e311ecd83b0419ebd4a6c1 temporarily removed the constant for a per-install secret in 11.26.3; 15772636355c6159d6c2dd6a608265ac65f4c208 restored it in 11.26.4 to repair inter-node communication. This closes both the explicit default branch and the subtle case where the in-memory/on-disk slot itself contains the default.

audit_record.bug_semantics: ERC7984's encrypted uint64 total-supply update deliberately turns an overflowing mint into a zero transfer rather than reverting. ERC7984ERC20Wrapper's wrap and ERC-1363 callback paths transfer or have already received the underlying ERC-20 before calling _mint, ignore _mint's returned transferred amount, and still complete. Once confidential total supply is full, a user therefore pays underlying tokens but receives no wrapped confidential tokens.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The wrapper's incorrect success assumption originated in the first decomposed member of squash PR #11: it introduced both wrapper entry paths with an unchecked _mint after underlying custody had moved. The base token's pre-existing _update/tryIncrease contract already exposed failure through a zero return, so the wrapper caller—not the saturating encrypted arithmetic—introduced the loss-of-funds composition flaw.

audit_record.evidence: First-party advisory https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-confidential-contracts/security/advisories/GHSA-hqf9-8xv5-x8xw states <=0.3.0 is affected and 0.3.1 is patched, explaining that euint64 total-supply overflow makes _mint fail silently while wrap/onTransferReceived do not check its result. PR #11's first-party commits API lists six members; local git show of 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be shows it created contracts/token/extensions/ConfidentialFungibleTokenERC20Wrapper.sol. At BIC lines 41 and 46-47, onTransferReceived calls _mint without its return and wrap calls safeTransferFrom before an unchecked _mint. In the same BIC tree, contracts/token/ConfidentialFungibleToken.sol:205 calls tryIncrease(_totalSupply, amount), and line 215 selects amount or encrypted zero into transferred. Later member e2adee4c7dee6a214fb10194daf0133d88bf8312 corrected imports/value/rate details but retained both flawed paths, so it was not the first writer. The final member 214750ca57768e2ad8e22b05658d2f0e8517421a and landed squash cb6a8a7bcc27352530164817c8b68333336f22c3 have the identical wrapper blob ee62576997e35beaa7112a0a03d8d5c08bffc657, proving decomposition linkage. `git tag --contains cb6a8a7...` includes v0.1.0, v0.2.0 and vulnerable boundary v0.3.0. Release-branch fix c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a (https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-confidential-contracts/commit/c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a) has v0.3.0 commit f0914b66f9f3766915403587b1ef1432d53054d3 as parent, adds ERC7984TotalSupplyOverflow and an _update mint guard based on underlying balance/rate, and is contained by v0.3.1 and v0.3.2. Original upstream fix 2484df01ca18fd5143dae744f46aac0bf8a2b43b has the identical fixed wrapper blob 833f124cad6087c1633013d88efe483614c14ef2 and is contained by v0.4.0 and later tags. `git cat-file commit 58f350da...` supplies the BIC-only attribution check stated in ai_marker.
audit_record.reasoning: The lifecycle begins with decomposed PR #11 member 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be, not its later squash carrier cb6a8a7bcc27352530164817c8b68333336f22c3. Subsequent PR members only made the initial wrapper compile, adjusted conversion math, tested, and polished it; the final member's wrapper blob exactly equals the landed squash blob. That carrier shipped by v0.1.0 and remains ancestral to v0.3.0. The v0.3 release-line patch c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a detects an inferred supply beyond uint64 capacity and reverts from the mint update; transaction atomicity then rolls back the underlying transfer/callback, closing the loss path in v0.3.1. Because the raw commit object of the smallest BIC names only a human author/committer and contains no AI attribution trailer or bot marker, later repository AI markers are irrelevant under the BIC-only rule and the closed verdict is NOT_AI.

review_record.bug_semantics: ERC7984 stores confidential total supply in an euint64. On overflow, its mint path selects a transferred amount of zero and leaves supply unchanged rather than reverting. ERC7984ERC20Wrapper's wrap path first transfers the caller's underlying ERC-20 into the wrapper, while its ERC-1363 callback runs after the underlying transfer; both paths then call _mint and ignore the returned actual amount. Once the confidential supply is full, the transaction therefore succeeds with the underlying tokens retained but zero confidential wrapped tokens minted, causing user fund loss.
review_record.flaw_origin: The unsafe composition first appears in PR #11 member commit 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be: it creates ConfidentialFungibleTokenERC20Wrapper and adds both the transfer-then-_mint wrap path and the onTransferReceived _mint path without consuming or checking _mint's return value. The parent already had the intentionally non-reverting encrypted overflow behavior in ConfidentialFungibleToken, but had no ERC-20 wrapper, so the loss-of-funds mechanism did not yet exist.

review_record.evidence: Advisory https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-confidential-contracts/security/advisories/GHSA-hqf9-8xv5-x8xw states the exact silent euint64 overflow/ignored _mint return mechanism, affected <=0.3.0, and patched 0.3.1. In the clone, `git show 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be -- contracts/token/extensions/ConfidentialFungibleTokenERC20Wrapper.sol` shows the new wrapper, SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom followed by unchecked _mint in wrap, and unchecked _mint in onTransferReceived. `git grep -n -C 4 -e 'function tryIncrease' -e 'function _mint' -e 'transferred = success.select' e1516e341eaae579028ab3b61523ef4d606457bc -- contracts/token/ConfidentialFungibleToken.sol` shows the pre-existing parent behavior: overflow success is computed by newValue >= oldValue, _mint returns _update, and failure selects zero. PR #11's first-party commits endpoint, https://api.github.com/repos/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-confidential-contracts/pulls/11/commits, decomposes landed squash cb6a8a7bcc27352530164817c8b68333336f22c3 into the six listed member SHAs. Across that member chain, `git log --reverse -S'_mint(to,' 214750ca57768e2ad8e22b05658d2f0e8517421a -- contracts/token/extensions/ConfidentialFungibleTokenERC20Wrapper.sol` and the corresponding -S'SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom' query both return 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be as the first writer; `git log -L 31,48:contracts/token/extensions/ConfidentialFungibleTokenERC20Wrapper.sol 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be` agrees. `git ls-tree -r e1516e341eaae579028ab3b61523ef4d606457bc -- contracts/token/extensions/ConfidentialFungibleTokenERC20Wrapper.sol contracts/token/ERC7984/extensions/ERC7984ERC20Wrapper.sol` is empty, directly proving parent absence. The squash landed before v0.1.0 (tag commit 71202e4b38786097fbe2e2d190940d32eda1fd69). For the closing boundary, v0.3.0 resolves to f0914b66f9f3766915403587b1ef1432d53054d3 and is the direct parent of c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a; `git show c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a` adds ERC7984TotalSupplyOverflow and an _update override that checks inferred underlying-backed supply before minting. `git grep ERC7984TotalSupplyOverflow v0.3.0 -- contracts/token/ERC7984/extensions/ERC7984ERC20Wrapper.sol` is empty, while the same query at v0.3.1 shows the error/check/override; v0.3.1 resolves to 14f20de697573d815c1bf7cd7e67f386de08707f, contains c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a, and its package.json reports 0.3.1. The same patch also landed on the mainline as 2484df01ca18fd5143dae744f46aac0bf8a2b43b, but c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a is the direct fix on the affected v0.3 release line.
review_record.reasoning: The smallest real BIC is the first PR-member commit, not GitHub's later squash object: 58f350da0359bc8de8d6a0a97e9ea35b664b44be is atomic for this mechanism, its immediate parent has no wrapper, and later members only refine the newly introduced wrapper. The defect is the wrapper's failure to honor an existing zero-on-overflow _mint contract after accepting underlying assets. Commit c620d4386021dde63ae3ea1507dee8543791134a directly closes that mechanism on the vulnerable v0.3 line by making mint overflow synchronously revert, and it is included in the first patched release v0.3.1. Because the BIC commit object is authored and committed by a human and contains no qualifying AI marker, the evidence supports NOT_AI rather than either AI verdict.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The remotely reachable GET /api/artifacts endpoint reads the attacker-controlled id query parameter and interpolates it into the path of a Cloudflare KV API URL. URL normalization resolves ../ segments before fetch sends the request, so seven traversal segments can escape /accounts/{account}/storage/kv/namespaces/{namespace}/values and select another Cloudflare API path under /client/v4. The same fetch attaches the server's CLOUDFLARE_KV_API_KEY Bearer token and streams the upstream response back to the requester, producing authenticated SSRF and possible Cloudflare data or infrastructure exposure.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 421bf33c0e033ae5ab51f08902d9aa420f5b3f65 created app/api/artifact/route.ts and, in the initial implementation, combined all causal elements: unsanitized id input at line 34, direct URL-path interpolation through storeUrl(id) at lines 7-8 and 35, privileged Authorization at lines 9-10 and 36, and passthrough of the Cloudflare response at lines 39-43. Later commit d8afd1af88038d859b322fd55773c31d2cb6c4db only refactored the same vulnerable URL construction to `${storeUrl()}/values/${id}`; rename commit 6737f016f5c3d4ddc01a7b29ebb3b5df17138b96 only moved artifact to artifacts.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the raw BIC commit object names author and committer lloydzhou <lloydzhou@qq.com> and its message is only `save artifact content to cloudflare workers kv`; it has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, AI-assistant, or bot marker/trailer.
evidence: First-party disclosure https://github.com/ChatGPTNextWeb/NextChat/issues/6741 (source gist https://gist.github.com/YLChen-007/43252d45d75e8bdd2d45136fd6ffe8a5) identifies app/api/artifacts/route.ts, the ../../../../../../../user/tokens/verify traversal payload, automatic CLOUDFLARE_KV_API_KEY forwarding, affected versions through v2.16.1, and no patched version.

`git log --all --follow -- app/api/artifacts/route.ts` traces the file through the 100% rename at 6737f016f5c3d4ddc01a7b29ebb3b5df17138b96 to its creation in 421bf33c0e033ae5ab51f08902d9aa420f5b3f65; `git log --all --follow -p -G 'searchParams.*get("id")|storeUrl.*values'` shows 421bf33c0e033ae5ab51f08902d9aa420f5b3f65 first writing the vulnerable GET path and d8afd1af88038d859b322fd55773c31d2cb6c4db merely preserving it in refactored syntax.

`git cat-file -e 1ecefd88f741a22e83029a33d42232b69e27dddd:app/api/artifact/route.ts` and the corresponding artifacts path both fail because neither route exists in the immediate parent tree; the BIC diff creates app/api/artifact/route.ts from /dev/null.

Version ancestry establishes the boundary: BIC 421bf33c0e033ae5ab51f08902d9aa420f5b3f65 is not an ancestor of v2.13.1 (e079f1b31ab8cfb262a37e7ddf8ab0bf03a35464), is an ancestor of v2.14.0 (8b513537b7e9755ec3ede1de30a791fd579ecedc), and `git tag --contains` lists v2.14.0 through v2.16.1. Both v2.14.0 and v2.16.1 contain the unsanitized id-to-fetch path.

The validated origin/main tip defdcdb55d850cd12c4c657eb83729fd66e215c0 dated 2026-08-11 still has app/api/artifacts/route.ts blob 4707e795f0acef275a352d5c941e3e123591bb57 with `fetch(`${storeUrl()}/values/${id}`, { headers: storeHeaders() })`; all inspected origin refs carrying the endpoint use that same vulnerable blob, so no public fix commit exists in the supplied full-history clone.

`git cat-file -p 421bf33c0e033ae5ab51f08902d9aa420f5b3f65` provides the BIC-only attribution evidence: human author/committer lloydzhou <lloydzhou@qq.com>, one parent 1ecefd88f741a22e83029a33d42232b69e27dddd, and no AI-related commit-object trailer or marker.
audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerability begins with the endpoint itself, not with the next-day TTL refactor or the later singular-to-plural rename. The initial route commit accepts id from the query string, places it in a privileged Cloudflare API URL without validation or encoding, sends the deployment's Bearer token, and returns the selected upstream response; therefore it is the smallest real BIC. Its immediate parent lacks both possible route paths, proving parent absence. Release ancestry places the first vulnerable release at v2.14.0, after v2.13.1, and the same mechanism remains in the advisory's terminal affected tag v2.16.1 and in the validated 2026-08-11 main tip. There is no squash or member history to decompose. Because only the BIC commit object controls AI attribution and that object has a human author/committer with no AI marker or trailer, the causal verdict is NOT_AI. The issue, advisory, full ref history, and current main all indicate that the vulnerability remains unpatched, so fix_sha and direct_fix_sha are necessarily null rather than unknown.
audit_record.remaining_gap: Upstream remains unpatched: the disclosure names no patched version and the validated public-history main tip still contains the vulnerable endpoint, so there is no fix or direct-fix commit SHA to record.

audit_record.bug_semantics: On a server-capable NextChat deployment, app/mcp/actions.ts is a Next.js Server Action module because it begins with "use server". An unauthenticated caller can therefore supply an MCP configuration containing an arbitrary command, args, and env, persist it, and cause initialization to pass it to StdioClientTransport and client.connect(), spawning the process. The first form required invoking exported updateMcpConfig and then exported restartAllClients; the advisory-named later form, exported addMcpServer(clientId, config), performs persistence and initialization in one request. Neither form enforces authentication, authorization, ENABLE_MCP, or a command allowlist.

primary_record.bug_semantics: Because app/mcp/actions.ts begins with the Next.js "use server" directive, its exported async addMcpServer(clientId, config) function is remotely invocable as a Server Action. audit_record.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated request to /api/<unrecognized-provider>/<path> reaches the provider route's default branch, which invokes proxyHandler. proxyHandler constructs fetchUrl by concatenating the entirely client-controlled x-base-url header with the requested path and query string, performs fetch(fetchUrl, ...), and streams the upstream response back to the requester. Because neither the fallback nor proxyHandler restricts schemes, hosts, loopback/private/link-local addresses, redirects, or allowed plugin origins, a remote caller can make the server request internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or arbitrary external hosts and read the response, producing SSRF/open-proxy behavior.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit f652f7326070dfbffcc5f90a999e95df21f4c650 added plugin proxy/auth support as one single-parent commit. It created app/api/proxy.ts with the vulnerable x-base-url-to-fetchUrl data flow and, in app/api/[provider]/[...path]/route.ts, changed the switch so known OpenAI requests retain openaiHandler while every unknown provider is sent to the new proxyHandler. primary_record.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated request to /api/<unrecognized-provider>/<path> reaches the provider route's default branch, which invokes proxyHandler. proxyHandler constructs fetchUrl by concatenating the entirely client-controlled x-base-url header with the requested path and query string, performs fetch(fetchUrl, ...), and streams the upstream response back to the requester. Because neither the fallback nor proxyHandler restricts schemes, hosts, loopback/private/link-local addresses, redirects, or allowed plugin origins, a remote caller can make the server request internal services, cloud metadata endpoints, or arbitrary external hosts and read the response, producing SSRF/open-proxy behavior.

review_record.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated request to /api/<unrecognized-provider>/<path> reaches the dynamic provider route's default branch, which calls proxyHandler. proxyHandler constructs its fetch destination directly from the attacker-controlled x-base-url header plus attacker-controlled path/query data, performs the server-side fetch without an allowlist or private/loopback-address rejection, and streams the upstream response back. An attacker can therefore make the NextChat server request arbitrary external or internal resources, including loopback and cloud metadata endpoints.

The pre-existing route instead sent its default branch to the fixed OpenAI handler, and app/api/proxy.ts did not exist in the immediate parent.

audit_record.bug_semantics: In non-export deployments, Next.js attaches Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every /api/:path* response and, by v2.16.1, also advertises wildcard methods and request headers. An attacker-controlled web origin can therefore read non-credentialed API responses and send normally preflight-restricted headers. In the reported high-impact chain, cross-origin JavaScript supplies x-base-url to the unauthenticated fallback proxy; app/api/proxy.ts builds the server-side destination from that header and injects the configured OpenAI key whenever the supplied value contains api.openai.com, allowing cross-origin SSRF and reflected key disclosure. The invalid Allow-Credentials: true plus wildcard-origin combination does not make credentialed wildcard fetches work in modern browsers, but credentials are unnecessary for the exposed read/proxy path.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 50cd33dbb2992066dae8c51c2da6ef4781e4500a first created nextConfig.headers for non-export builds and applied Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * (plus Allow-Credentials: true) to /:path*, thereby first granting every web origin read access across the application, including API routes. Its immediate parent had no response-header policy at all. Commit 0fb775d71a0fac5ce4aa802bc3eb0b066c12ed7b then scoped the rule to /api/:path* while widening Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers to * and adding a one-day max age, which intensified the later x-base-url attack but did not originate the permissive-origin flaw. Commit 6f83fbd21278c90cd978108abe54291c38ec10d7 only extracted the unchanged headers into CorsHeaders and is a move/refactor, not the BIC.

Current app/api/[provider]/[...path]/route.ts:58-59 sends unknown providers to proxyHandler; app/api/proxy.ts:19-22 constructs fetchUrl from x-base-url, lines 37-46 conditionally install the server API key, and line 68 performs the fetch. Version check: `git for-each-ref --contains=50cd... --sort=version:refname refs/tags` reports v2.8 (2593de587224359ca86a22b0b7b143d4e54af315) as the first normal release tag containing the BIC; `git merge-base 50cd... v2.16.1^{commit}` returns the BIC, and v2.16.1 resolves to 557a2cce357749c6fb3176d42e03ff6f7de4d355. `git show v2.16.1:next.config.mjs` contains the exact wildcard-origin/method/header policy. The associated #1000 work sought browser/client-side operation, consistent with a functional CORS motivation, but does not alter the causal diff. The next-day 0fb775d71a0fac5ce4aa802bc3eb0b066c12ed7b deliberately made the API preflight maximally permissive, enabling arbitrary custom headers; later proxy functionality made x-base-url a server-side destination control and created the reported SSRF/key-disclosure chain. Tag ancestry and snapshots prove the flaw shipped by v2.8 and remained in the advisory's v2.16.1 boundary. The validated main snapshot remains vulnerable after the report, so fix_sha and direct_fix_sha are justified nulls and the case is explicitly unpatched. Finally, the only admissible AI evidence is the 50cd commit object; it has a human author/committer and no AI marker, yielding NOT_AI regardless of later commits or issue text.

review_record.bug_semantics: For non-export builds, NextChat's Next.js response-header rule grants Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to the API surface. The current rule also grants every method and request header, so JavaScript from an attacker-controlled origin can pass preflight, send custom headers, and read API responses. In the reported high-impact chain, the permitted x-base-url header reaches the catch-all /api/[provider]/[...path] route; an unknown provider falls through to app/api/proxy.ts, which constructs a server-side fetch URL from x-base-url and injects the configured OpenAI key when that attacker-controlled string contains api.openai.com. The wildcard origin is the underlying CWE-346/CWE-942 flaw; wildcard methods/headers and the unauthenticated proxy amplify its consequences.
review_record.flaw_origin: Commit 50cd33dbb2992066dae8c51c2da6ef4781e4500a is the smallest true BIC: it first added nextConfig.headers for non-export builds, matched /:path* (therefore including API routes), and emitted Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true. Its parent e6b49a60c0eba9e591546a419eed5ed389c44b43 has no nextConfig.headers callback or CORS response headers. Commit 0fb775d71a0fac5ce4aa802bc3eb0b066c12ed7b one day later narrowed the rule to /api/:path* but amplified it by changing Allow-Methods and Allow-Headers to * and adding a 24-hour max age; it did not first create the untrusted-origin policy. Commit 6f83fbd21278c90cd978108abe54291c38ec10d7 merely moved the already-vulnerable header array into CorsHeaders and is rejected as a refactor BIC.

review_record.bug_semantics: The affected SDK methods insert caller-influenced identifiers directly into URL path template literals while attaching the merchant's bearer token. Slash or dot-dot content can be normalized by the WHATWG URL parser into a different API path, and a question mark can become attacker-chosen query syntax, so an application that passes an untrusted identifier without its own ownership check can make credentialed requests outside the intended resource. The affected families are payment get/capture/cancel, paymentRefund create/total/list/get, advancedPayment get/capture/cancel/update/updateReleaseDate, and disbursementRefund create/createAll/listAll.
review_record.flaw_origin: The smallest first mainline change among the advisory's affected methods is 7d83325f4760a079a0d3f3f69001c07a8d380657 ('payment refund client'). It created the payment-refund create/get/list implementations and directly interpolated payment_id (and refund_id for get) into /v1/payments/... paths. Later additions extended the same pre-existing flaw: payment capture in 6008b53014be88d6757e89ec42688ce7d8906fe0, cancel in 0fdb24947c5f0e211d49e6d169f53b461c1dc2c3, get in 203000cd6d49d416ff8a50ca4cae290da4b92b13, refund total in 3c58ca7b51d8917681b56d5ae17265d21c047d4c, and the advancedPayment/disbursementRefund clients in adcaceaa233f5c7cb67d4723d6b7ca0cfdd25e2b. audit_record.bug_semantics: An attacker who can post to a Telegram group can store HTML in a message's content. The search/list UI passed that database-backed item.content to highlightKeyword(), which returned the text unchanged when no keyword was present and otherwise performed only a regex replacement that inserted a highlight span; neither branch escaped the message text. review_record.bug_semantics: Stored cross-site scripting in Telegram message search results: an attacker who can post to a shared Telegram group can store markup such as as message content. The application persists that content and later passes item.content to highlightKeyword(), which returned the raw text with only matching substrings wrapped in a span; Vue's v-html then assigned that attacker-controlled string as innerHTML. Merely rendering the result in another user's browser executes the handler. The closing change HTML-escapes message text before adding the intended highlight markup and also HTML/regex-escapes the keyword.
review_record.flaw_origin: The smallest first-writer is decomposed PR #145 member 6454fcaf810d2cd92d9010dffc6b14b3acfa0ad7 ('feat: global search', 2025-05-09). It created apps/frontend/src/components/GlobalSearch.vue, including highlightKeyword(text, keyword), the unescaped return text.replace(regex, '$1'), and v-html="highlightKeyword(item.content, keyword)". The mainline commit 4fec95f79a6215d61e92f572baefef9379632d55 is the squash aggregate, not the BIC. Later commits renamed, extracted, copied, and moved the same mechanism through SearchDialog.vue, MessageList.vue, packages/stage-ui, and apps/web; those are not first introductions.

audit_record.bug_semantics: In policycoreutils/scripts/fixfiles, the DEFAULT restore path used find to select entries with unlabeled or undefined SELinux contexts and then invoked a separate privileged chcon process on each pathname. The non-full-cleanup relabel path reached the same code. An attacker controlling a searched directory could replace an intermediate component with a symlink after find checked the entry but before chcon resolved the pathname, causing an arbitrary target such as /etc/shadow to receive the attacker's chosen SELinux label. chcon --no-dereference protected only the final component and did not make the find-to-chcon pathname handoff atomic.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable find-then-chcon mechanism predates the validated Git history. Root object 13cd4c8960688af11ad23b4c946149015c80d549 is an aggregate snapshot named `initial import from svn trunk revision 2950`; it already contains the vulnerable /tmp and /var/tmp commands and has no Git parent. It is therefore a history boundary, not the smallest real BIC. Later commits only changed label selection, broadened the searched directories, moved the existing block, or added final-component --no-dereference handling without originating the race. The pre-r2950 Subversion member revision that first wrote the mechanism is unavailable in the clone.
audit_record.ai_marker: unavailable: the smallest real BIC is a pre-r2950 Subversion member revision with no commit object in the validated Git clone, so its author, committer, message, trailers, and bot identity cannot be inspected; the no-AI metadata on aggregate import 13cd4c8960688af11ad23b4c946149015c80d549 is excluded because that object is not the BIC
evidence: The assigned GHSA bundle describes CWE-367 in fixfiles relabel/restore: a local attacker races the find/chcon handoff by replacing directory components with symlinks, allowing privileged relabeling of arbitrary files. The bundle reports no package-version ranges and identifies a556538c2d5d2583273e025b45c02651fef47679 as the upstream fix.

`git show --format=fuller --stat --patch a556538c2d5d2583273e025b45c02651fef47679 -- policycoreutils/scripts/fixfiles` shows a one-file direct fix deleting all ten cleanup lines. Its message says that find and chcon re-look up full pathnames and are subject to TOCTOU. `git rev-parse a556538c2d5d2583273e025b45c02651fef47679^` returns 7fd20e48504069fe1541f809de7566283f8ec7db.

primary_record.bug_semantics: When an administrator runs `fixfiles restore` or the non-full-cleanup path of `fixfiles relabel`, the DEFAULT restore path first has `find` select entries with an unlabeled or undefined SELinux context and then invokes a separate `chcon` process on each pathname. A local attacker controlling a searched directory can replace an intermediate path component with a symlink after `find` checks the entry but before `chcon` resolves the pathname. `chcon --no-dereference` protects only against dereferencing a symlink in the final pathname component; it does not prevent traversal through a swapped intermediate symlink, so the privileged process can change the SELinux label of an arbitrary target such as `/etc/shadow`.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The PATCH /api/customers/:id endpoint is reachable without an authenticated admin or customer session and trusts the attacker-controlled path UUID as the record to update. Its only route-local middleware parses JSON; the handler selects that UUID, spreads attacker-controlled fields (including email and password) into the customer update, and returns the updated record without checking that the caller owns the customer, enabling unauthenticated account takeover and lockout.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit a2f514ad10073fb9ae164446f30205086151c095 first made the predeclared /customers/:id route operational by adding updateCustomer.js and body-parser middleware while simultaneously adding the global API auth middleware whose explicit rule treated every route with no access property as public. The route then had no access property, so the new mutating handler was unauthenticated from its first executable revision. Commit 4b97829de4acc674cd2282af3d2b61ec3416f72b later changed the default to private but explicitly labeled this route public, preserving rather than originating the flaw.

audit_record.bug_semantics: tcpliveplay accepts a user-supplied pcap, obtains an IPv4 header from libpcap's caplen-bounded packet buffer, and rewrites the packet before replay. fix_all_checksum_liveplay derives the TCP checksum length solely from the packet-controlled IPv4 total-length field (ntohs(ip_len) minus ip_hl) without proving that the claimed length fits the captured buffer. do_checksum_liveplay forwards that length to do_checksum_math_liveplay, whose loop reads successive 16-bit words until the claimed length is exhausted. A crafted pcap can therefore claim an IP length larger than caplen and make the checksum loop read past libpcap's heap buffer, causing the reported heap-buffer-overflow and denial of service.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 0b287ed9052f740ecb04df556dd07f03c4186e01 imported tcpliveplay.c as a new 1,303-line file and, in the same commit, added the complete vulnerable path: main calls rewrite on argv[2], rewrite consumes pcap_next_ex packet buffers and calls fix_all_checksum_newconn, fix_all_checksum_newconn trusts ip_len for the checksum length, and do_checksum_math_newconn walks that length without a caplen bound. Later commits only renamed the *_newconn helpers to *_liveplay or reformatted the same calculation, so the import commit is the smallest repository commit that first wrote the flawed mechanism.

review_record.bug_semantics: tcpliveplay accepts a user-supplied pcap, obtains each packet from libpcap, rewrites its headers, and recalculates checksums. fix_all_checksum_liveplay derives the TCP checksum length solely from the untrusted IPv4 total-length/header-length fields as ntohs(iphdr->ip_len) - (iphdr->ip_hl << 2), without bounding that result by the pcap record's caplen. do_checksum_liveplay passes this length to do_checksum_math_liveplay, whose 16-bit loop reads that many bytes from the TCP-header pointer. A crafted pcap can therefore make the loop read beyond libpcap's heap packet buffer, causing the reported heap-buffer-overflow and denial of service.
review_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable checksum-length trust and unbounded checksum loop entered tcpreplay together when the externally developed tcpliveplay source was first imported as a new file in commit 0b287ed9052f740ecb04df556dd07f03c4186e01. Later commits e5039a91fbf018b5c7d084224c884e2275529724 (function rename) and 8f3761d212d39d82a3f2cad39f9f92c1ebc3ca5c (cleanup/formatting) preserved the same flaw and are not introducers.

First-party issue https://github.com/appneta/tcpreplay/issues/925 gives the ASan reproduction on 4.5.1: rewrite -> fix_all_checksum_liveplay -> do_checksum_liveplay -> do_checksum_math_liveplay, a READ of size 2 exactly past a 2048-byte libpcap heap allocation. The issue is labeled `shelved` (`Will not be addressed in foreseeable future`); maintainer comments on 2025-07-12 say no more tcpliveplay updates and close it without a code fix.

audit_record.bug_semantics: HPE OneView exposes PUT /rest/id-pools/executeCommand without authentication. The controller deserializes the request JSON as an ExecutableCommand and passes its attacker-controlled cmd value to RuntimeExecutorService.execute, which invokes Java Runtime.exec. An unauthenticated network attacker can therefore execute arbitrary commands in the appliance's Trusted RM Container context when the ID Pools endpoint is enabled.
audit_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable implementation is proprietary HPE OneView appliance code in guidserver.jar, specifically PoolController.executeCommand and RuntimeExecutorService, not code in rapid7/metasploit-framework. review_record.bug_semantics: HPE OneView exposes PUT /rest/id-pools/executeCommand without authentication. The request JSON is deserialized as an ExecutableCommand; PoolController.executeCommand passes its attacker-controlled cmd property to RuntimeExecutorService.execute, which invokes Java Runtime.exec. A remote unauthenticated caller can therefore execute an arbitrary command (Rapid7 demonstrated a reverse shell as the trm3 Trusted RM Container user). Endpoint availability limits practical exposure: Rapid7 found it enabled on OneView for VMs 6.x and likely all unpatched OneView for HPE Synergy versions, while some other VM editions return 404 because ID Pools is disabled. HPE's official affected-products statement nevertheless lists all HPE OneView versions through 10.20.
review_record.flaw_origin: The vulnerable implementation is proprietary HPE OneView appliance code in guidserver.jar (com.hp.ci.mgmt.guidpools.controllers.PoolController plus RuntimeExecutorService), not code in rapid7/metasploit-framework. This repository contains a post-disclosure Metasploit exploit client and documentation only. The smallest true BIC would be the HPE source-history change that first combined unauthenticated reachability with execution of the request-controlled cmd value, but HPE's source repository and commit history are not public in the assigned evidence.
review_record.ai_marker: Not assessable: the true HPE OneView BIC commit object is unavailable, so there is no BIC author/committer identity or trailer block to inspect. No AI inference is made from the Rapid7 exploit commit a4dba967122de40dc3e4cba554dc4fa2be73ca48 because it post-dates disclosure and adds an exploit for the external flaw rather than introducing the vulnerable vendor code.
review_record.evidence: Vendor/version boundary: open https://support.hpe.com/hpesc/public/docDisplay?docId=hpesbgn04985en_us&docLocale=en_US and inspect HPESBGN04985 rev.4 (release date 2025-12-16, last updated 2026-01-31). Its affected-products section says 'HPE OneView - All versions through v10.20'; its resolution says v11.00 or later addresses the vulnerability and an updated security hotfix applies to versions 5.20 through 10.20, superseding the earlier Z7550-98077 hotfix. Mechanism/fix behavior: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-cve-2025-37164-analysis/ reproduces the decompiled NO_AUTH PoolController.executeCommand method, the attacker-controlled ExecutableCommand.cmd flow into Runtime.getRuntime().exec, a successful unauthenticated reverse-shell request, and the vendor hotfix's Apache rule `RewriteRule ^/rest/id-pools/executeCommand$ - [R=404,L]`. The earlier Rapid7 notice at https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/etr-cve-2025-37164-critical-unauthenticated-rce-affecting-hewlett-packard-enterprise-oneview/ likewise identifies the endpoint, pre-11.0/5.20-10.20 boundary, and emergency binary hotfixes. Repository disambiguation (run in the assigned clone): `git log --follow --format='%H %P %aI %s' -- modules/exploits/linux/http/hpe_oneview_rce.rb` shows only a4dba967122de40dc3e4cba554dc4fa2be73ca48 and two same-day follow-ups; `git log --all --reverse --format='%H %P %aI %s' -S'executeCommand' -- modules/exploits/linux/http/hpe_oneview_rce.rb` returns a4dba967122de40dc3e4cba554dc4fa2be73ca48, parent 2bb30ba7a3eae4560a7e8ac34e09339804ddef2e, dated 2025-12-19, with subject 'add in the HPE OneView exploit'; `git log -L 143,157:modules/exploits/linux/http/hpe_oneview_rce.rb` shows that commit adding execute_cmd from /dev/null; and `git ls-tree -r --name-only 2bb30ba7a3eae4560a7e8ac34e09339804ddef2e -- modules/exploits/linux/http/hpe_oneview_rce.rb` is empty. `git show --format=fuller --stat a4dba967122de40dc3e4cba554dc4fa2be73ca48` shows a 404-line exploit/module-documentation addition after vendor disclosure, and `git describe --contains --tags a4dba967122de40dc3e4cba554dc4fa2be73ca48` returns `6.4.104~4^2~3`; these establish only the Metasploit exploit lifecycle, not a vulnerability BIC or vendor fix. Searching the clone for PoolController, RuntimeExecutorService, or com.hp.ci.mgmt.guidpools returns no vendor implementation. Thus no Git commit in this clone is the true introducer or direct fix, while the actual remediation is distributed by HPE as appliance release 11.00 and binary/config hotfixes rather than a public source commit.
review_record.reasoning: Vulnerability-first tracing places both causal components in HPE's closed appliance: an endpoint explicitly marked NO_AUTH and a controller/service path that executes the request body's cmd without an authorization or command-policy barrier. The revised hotfix closes the network path by forcing the endpoint to 404, and 11.00 is the first vendor-declared fixed release. The Rapid7 repository was linked by the advisory because it supplies exploit code; its earliest relevant commit landed three days after disclosure and its direct parent lacks the module, so treating that commit as the BIC would invert cause and proof-of-concept. Because neither the source change that introduced the HPE behavior nor the source change behind the vendor fix is publicly represented by a commit object, the smallest BIC, its immediate-parent absence, fix SHA, and BIC-only AI metadata cannot be established. This is a genuine proprietary-history boundary, so BLOCKED is more accurate than EVIDENCE_GAP and no NOT_AI/AI verdict is supportable.
review_record.remaining_gap: Blocked on non-public HPE OneView source/VCS history and commit objects for the vulnerable guidserver.jar implementation and the v11.00/hotfix remediation. Those records are required to identify the smallest true BIC, verify its immediate parent lacks the flaw, map the source-level direct fix, and inspect only the BIC commit object for AI authorship signals. Public appliance binaries and decompiled code prove behavior and release boundaries but cannot supply those commit-level facts.

audit_record.bug_semantics: A course student can bypass navigation/button hiding by directly loading /courses/{course-id}/settings#share or /courses/{course-id}/people?add=true. The settings route renders course-management settings without a route-level student-role guard, while the people invitation modal derives its open state from the user-controlled add=true query even though the ordinary Add button is role-gated. This is an object-keyed authorization failure, not merely hidden UI discoverability.

Because that boundary is a squash aggregate and none of its original CLASSROOMIO-T-90 member commit objects is present, the smallest real settings BIC cannot be named. The later invite-query surface is independently decomposable: 0b61becdbe1e5d4f7c5d03a3819ff4e0b6792d1a, not its parent 9f04d4e3a7dd3335ea8fc7db10efe78eab1431a7, first makes add=true itself open the modal; that later BIC cannot replace the unavailable earlier BIC for the advisory's combined vulnerability.

primary_record.bug_semantics: Course-management authorization was enforced only by hiding navigation and buttons, not by guarding the management routes or the URL-controlled modal. A student who is a legitimate course member can supply a course ID and browse /courses/{id}/settings#share or /courses/{id}/people?add=true; the course layout admits any course member, the settings route renders its management component, and the add=true query value alone opens the invitation dialog containing tutor-selection and student invite-link controls.

review_record.bug_semantics: getRecommendTitleFromMarkdownString applies /#{1,6} {1,}(.*\S.*)(?:\n|$)/g to renderer-supplied Markdown when the Electron main process handles save and save-as. audit_record.bug_semantics: A crafted Juniper-Ethernet pcap can advertise unsupported extension media/encapsulation while still being long enough for dlt_jnpr_ether_decode() to treat the post-extension bytes as Ethernet. A successful en10mb subdecoder decode is followed by tcpedit_dlt_copy_decoder_state(), which assigns the subcontext-owned decoded_extra allocation directly to the outer context. Cleanup then traverses the outer context and the recursively owned subcontext; dlt_linuxsll2_cleanup() frees each context's decoded_extra pointer, so the aliased allocation is freed twice and tcprewrite aborts or corrupts memory.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 745a71184c9d739305d4319cf2e6bb3998cc27b6 introduced the Juniper subdecoder lifecycle as one cohesive feature: it created an en10mb subcontext, copied subdecoder state by borrowing the decoded_extra pointer without transferring or recording ownership, and recursively destroyed the subcontext during outer cleanup. It also continued to decode Juniper payloads as Ethernet without validating the extension-declared media type and encapsulation. Those combined lines first created the aliased-ownership double-free path; later aggregate/import commit 77387f1580220c1232a9091c79d0db83ba7ac5b0 merely reintroduced the already-existing mechanism into the 4.0 line.
audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the BIC commit object names Aaron Turner <synfinatic@gmail.com> as both author and committer and contains only the subject/body 'add support for subdecoders refs #389 / improve JUNIPER_ETHERNET_DLT refs #387'; it has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, Assisted-by, bot identity, or other AI trailer.
evidence: First-party issue https://github.com/appneta/tcpreplay/issues/926 reports the ASan double free in tcprewrite 4.5.1: dlt_linuxsll2_cleanup() frees the allocation, outer tcpedit_dlt_cleanup() reaches dlt_jnpr_ether_cleanup(), and the nested tcpedit_dlt_cleanup() reaches dlt_linuxsll2_cleanup() again. Maintainer Fred Klassen states the reproducer is fixed by issue #902 and shows 4.5.2 rejecting the unsupported packet with a decoder warning.
NVD https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-51006 describes the same crafted-pcap double free and lists Broadcom tcpreplay 4.5.1 as the affected CPE.

primary_record.bug_semantics: A crafted Juniper-Ethernet pcap can advertise unsupported extension media/encapsulation while still being long enough for dlt_jnpr_ether_decode() to treat the post-extension bytes as Ethernet. A successful en10mb subdecoder decode is followed by tcpedit_dlt_copy_decoder_state(), which assigns the subcontext-owned decoded_extra allocation directly to the outer context. review_record.bug_semantics: A crafted DLT_JUNIPER_ETHER pcap processed by tcprewrite can reach the Juniper decoder's embedded Ethernet subdecoder. The subdecoder owns an allocated decoded_extra buffer, but tcpedit_dlt_copy_decoder_state() shallow-copies that pointer into the outer context without transferring or sharing ownership. At tcpedit_close(), both contexts are cleaned: in the reported 4.5.1 stack, dlt_linuxsll2_cleanup() runs once for the outer context and again while dlt_jnpr_ether_cleanup() recursively cleans the subcontext, freeing the same allocation twice and aborting under ASan. This is a local, user-assisted denial-of-service/memory-corruption path through a supplied capture file.

audit_record.bug_semantics: The REST frontend registered an /engine-ui proxy whose request path supplied both the destination host and port. EngineUIProxyServlet parsed /engine-ui/<host>:<port>/..., then constructed and issued an HTTP request to that destination without an enable/disable gate or destination allowlist. A remote requester able to reach the proxy could therefore make the Kyuubi server contact arbitrary hosts reachable from the server, yielding SSRF/open-proxy behavior.
